Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 1:

(p-388) Surat at-Tawbah

﴿Disavowal from Allah and His Messenger toward those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant.﴾

Section on its revelation

It is Madani by the consensus of the scholars, except for the last two verses, ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾, for they were revealed in Makkah. Al-Bukhari related in his Sahih, from the hadith of al-Bara', who said: "The last surah revealed in full was Bara'ah (al-Tawbah)." It is reported that one of the Arabs heard a reciter reciting this surah, and the Bedouin said: "I think this is among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an." He was asked: "How do you know that?" He said: "I hear covenants being cast off and injunctions being enforced."

Section

They differed concerning the first part of Bara'ah to be revealed, on three opinions.

The first: the first thing revealed from it was His saying: ﴿Certainly Allah has given you victory in many battlefields﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:25]. This was said by Mujahid.

(p-389) The second: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:41]. This was said by Abu al-Duha and Abu Malik.

The third: ﴿If you do not support him﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:40]. This was said by Muqatil. This disagreement concerns the first part of it revealed at Madinah, for they have said that the two verses at its end were revealed at Makkah.

Section

It has nine names. The first: Surat al-Tawbah (the Surah of Repentance). The second: Bara'ah (Disavowal); these two are well known among the people. The third: Surat al-'Adhab (the Surah of Punishment), said by Hudhayfah. The fourth: al-Muqashqishah (the Purifier), said by Ibn 'Umar. The fifth: Surat al-Buhuth (the Surah of Searching), because it searched into the secrets of the hypocrites, said by al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. The sixth: al-Fadihah (the Exposer), because it exposed the hypocrites, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The seventh: al-Mubaʿthirah (the Scatterer), because it scattered the reports about people and uncovered their secrets, said by al-Harith ibn Yazid and Ibn Ishaq. The eighth: al-Muthirah (the Stirrer), because it stirred up the disgraces and faults of the hypocrites, said by Qatadah. The ninth: al-Hafirah (the Digger), because it dug into the hearts of the hypocrites, said by al-Zajjaj.

Section

Concerning the reason they did not write the basmalah at its beginning, there are three opinions.

The first: narrated by Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I said to 'Uthman ibn 'Affan: What led you to join al-Anfal, which is of the mathani (oft-repeated), and Bara'ah, which is of the mi'in (hundreds), placing them together, and you did not write between them 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate'?" He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when something was revealed to him, would call some of those who wrote, and say: 'Place this in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned.' al-Anfal was among the first of what was revealed at Madinah, and Bara'ah was among the last of the Qur'an, and their story resembled one another. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away without explaining to us that it was part of it, so we assumed it was part of it. For this reason they were joined together, and I did not write between them 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate'." A similar meaning is mentioned from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. al-Zajjaj said: "The resemblance between them is that al-Anfal mentions covenants and Bara'ah mentions their annulment." Qatadah used to say: "They are one surah."

The second: narrated by Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, who said: "I said to my father: Why did you not write in Bara'ah 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate'?" He said: "My son, Bara'ah was revealed with the sword, and 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate' is a security." Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah was asked about this and said: "Because the basmalah is mercy, and mercy is security, and this surah was revealed concerning the hypocrites."

The third: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote in the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate,' they did not accept it and rejected it, so Allah did not return it to them." This was said by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya al-Makki.

Section

As for the occasion of its revelation, the exegetes said: The Arabs began breaking covenants that they had made with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so Allah the Exalted commanded him to return their covenants to them. He revealed Bara'ah in the ninth year. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abu Bakr as commander over the pilgrimage season, to lead the people in Hajj that year, and sent with him a portion of Bara'ah to recite to the people of the season. When he had set out, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called 'Ali and said: "Go out with this account from the beginning of Bara'ah and proclaim it to the people." 'Ali went out on the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ she-camel al-'Adba' until he overtook Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr returned and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has something been revealed concerning me?" He said: "No, but none may convey on my behalf except a man from me. Are you not pleased that you were my companion in the cave, and that you will be my companion at the Pool?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." Abu Bakr then went on as commander of the Hajj, and 'Ali went on to proclaim Bara'ah.

Section

Concerning the number of verses which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent from the beginning of Bara'ah, there are five opinions. The first: forty verses, said by 'Ali, peace be upon him. The second: thirty verses, said by Abu Hurayrah. The third: ten verses, said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: seven verses, narrated by Ibn Jurayj from 'Ata'. The fifth: nine verses, said by Muqatil.

Section

If someone imagines that in taking Bara'ah from Abu Bakr and handing it to 'Ali there is a preference of 'Ali over Abu Bakr, he is mistaken, because the Prophet ﷺ conducted the Arabs in this matter according to their customs. al-Zajjaj said: "It has been the custom of the Arabs, in concluding their covenants and annulling them, that a man from the tribe takes charge of this. It is possible that the Arabs, when the annulment of the covenant was recited to them by someone not from the kin of the Prophet ﷺ, would say: 'This contradicts what we know of ourselves in the annulment of covenants,' so the Prophet ﷺ removed the objection by what he did." 'Amr ibn Bahr said: "This is not a preference of 'Ali over Abu Bakr; rather he dealt with them according to their well-known custom in dissolving agreements, and none would take charge of this except the chief among them, or a man of his kin who was close, such as a brother or an uncle. Abu Bakr was the imam in that pilgrimage and 'Ali followed him, Abu Bakr was the preacher and 'Ali listened." Abu Hurayrah said: "Abu Bakr sent me in that pilgrimage with the criers whom he sent to proclaim at Mina: that no polytheist should perform Hajj after this year, and none should circumambulate the House naked. 'Ali proclaimed Bara'ah with us and with those words." al-Sha'bi said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Ali to proclaim in four phrases: 'Beware, no polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year. Beware, none shall circumambulate the House naked. Beware, none shall enter Paradise except a Muslim. Beware, whoever has a term of agreement with Muhammad, his term extends to its period, and Allah is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger.'"

Section

As for the interpretation, His saying ﴿Disavowal﴾: al-Farra' said: it is in the nominative by the implied "this is" (hadhihi), like His saying ﴿A surah which We have sent down﴾ [al-Nur 24:1]. al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "I disassociated myself (bari'tu) from the man and from the religion, disavowal (bara'ah)," and "I was cured (bari'tu) of the illness"; and "bara'tu" also, "abra'u bur'an," and they have transmitted "barra'tu abarru burur," but we do not find in what has a hamzah as its third radical the pattern fa'altu af'alu except this word. And it is said: "bareetu al-qalam" (I sharpened the pen), and for everything you shave, "abriyhi bary," without hamzah. Abu Raja', Mawriq and Ibn Ya'mur read "bara'atan" in the accusative. The exegetes said: Disavowal here means: the severing of allegiance, the lifting of protection, and the removal of security. The address in His saying ﴿toward those with whom you made a covenant﴾ is to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and what is meant is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because he was the one who handled the covenant, and his companions were content; so by their contentment they also made the covenant. This is general for everyone who made a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Muqatil said: They are three tribes of the Arabs: Khuza'ah, Banu Mudlij, and Banu Judhaymah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾, meaning: move about in it secure, with no harm coming to you from Us.

If someone says: this is address to the present (second person), while the first verse is a report about an absent party (third person), so there are two answers to this.

The first: it is permissible among the Arabs to shift from the absent (third person) to direct address. ʿAntarah said:

﻿Far have become the visiting-places of the lovers, and your pursuit of Ibnat Makhram has become difficult for me.

This is the saying of Abu ʿUbaydah.

The second: there is an implied element in the speech, its sense being: "So say to them: Travel freely in the land," meaning: go about in it, advancing and retreating. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

They differed regarding those for whom these four months were granted, in four opinions.

(p-394) The first: they are a guarantee of safety for the people of covenants. Whoever's covenant was longer than these, his term was lowered to them; whoever's covenant was shorter than these, it was raised to them; and whoever had no covenant, his term was the end of Muharram, fifty nights. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second: they apply to the polytheists in general, both those with a covenant and those without one. This was said by Mujahid, al-Zuhri and al-Qurazi.

The third: it is a term for those whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had granted safety for less than four months, or whose safety was unlimited; as for one who had no safety, he is an enemy. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The fourth: it is a guarantee of safety for those who had neither safety nor covenant; as for the holders of covenants, they remain upon their covenants until their terms expire. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. It is confirmed by what is reported: that ʿAli proclaimed on that day: "Whoever has a covenant between himself and the Messenger of Allah, his covenant is until its term." In some wordings: "His term is four months." They differed regarding the period of these four months, in four opinions.

The first: they are the sacred months: Rajab, Dhu al-Qaʿdah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: their beginning is the Day of the Greater Hajj, which is the Day of Sacrifice (al-Nahr), and their end is the tenth of Rabiʿ al-Akhir. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Qurazi.

The third: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qaʿdah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram, because this verse was revealed in Shawwal. This was said by al-Zuhri. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: this is the weakest of the opinions, for had it been so, it would not have been permissible to delay informing them of it until Dhu al-Hijjah, since the command does not bind them until after they are informed.

The fourth: their beginning is the tenth of Dhu al-Qaʿdah and their end is the tenth of Rabiʿ al-Awwal, because the Hajj in that year fell on that day; then in the second year it fell in the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, and in that year the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed Hajj, and said: "Indeed time has come full circle." Al-Mawardi mentioned this.

(p-395) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, meaning: even if you are granted these four months, you will never escape Allah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the better reading is opening "anna" (with a fatha), meaning: "know that"; it is also permissible to read it with a kasra, as a new sentence. This is a guarantee from Allah of the support of the believers over the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿to the people﴾, meaning: to the people. It is said: "This is a notification for you and to you." Here "the people" is general, covering both the believers and the polytheists. Regarding "the Day of the Greater Hajj," there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the Day of 'Arafah. This was said by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abū Juḥayfah, Ṭāwūs, and ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: that it is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This was said by Abū Mūsā al-Ash'arī, al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah, ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Awfā, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Zayd, and al-Suddī, among others. It is also related from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās, in the manner of the two opinions.

The third: that it refers to all the days of the Hajj, so the day is used to express the days. This was said by Sufyān al-Thawrī. Sufyān said: just as it is said "the Day of Buʿāth," "the Day of the Camel," and "the Day of Ṣiffīn," meaning by it a period of days, since not every one of those wars lasted for days. It is also related from Mujāhid, in the manner of the three opinions.

Regarding its being named "the Greater Hajj," there are three opinions.

The first: that it was so named because it coincided in a year when the Muslims and the polytheists performed Hajj together, and that day coincided with the festival of the Jews and the Christians. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: that the Greater Hajj is the Hajj itself, and the Lesser is the ʿUmrah. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ and al-Shaʿbī.

The third: that the Greater Hajj is the Qur'an, and the Lesser is the Ifrād (performing Hajj alone, without ʿUmrah). This was said by Mujāhid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists﴾. al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Ibn Yaʿmur read "inna Allāha" with a kasrah on the hamzah, meaning: from the covenant of the polytheists, so the genitive noun was omitted.

"And His Messenger" is in the nominative, being the subject of a new sentence, and its predicate is implied, meaning: and His Messenger is also free of obligation. Abū Razīn, Abū Mijlaz, Abū Rajāʾ, Mujāhid, Ibn Yaʿmur, and Zayd, on the authority of Yaʿqūb, read "wa-rasūlahu" in the accusative. Then he returned to addressing the polytheists with His saying: from the faith.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 4:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾. Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas: When Ali recited "Bara'a" (the opening of Surah al-Tawba), the Banu Damra said: "Are we also like them?" He said: "No, because Allah, Exalted is He, has excepted you," and then he recited this verse. Mujahid said: They are a people who had a covenant and a term with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so He commanded that it be fulfilled for them. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the speech is: disavowal (bara'a) was issued toward those covenanted polytheists who broke the covenants, except those with whom you made a covenant and who did not break it with you; so they are not included in the disavowal as long as they do not break the covenant. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: The decisive word on this matter is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had a general covenant with all the polytheists, namely that no one would be barred from the House and no one would be feared in the sacred month; so Allah made their covenant four months. And between him and certain peoples among them there were covenants until specified terms, so He commanded that they be fulfilled for them and their term completed, provided he did not fear their treachery.

(p-398) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed⦆ — there are two views concerning it.

One is that they are Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram; this is the view of the majority.

The second is that they are the four months during which the polytheists were granted a respite for travel (al-siyahah, wandering through the land). This is the view of al-Hasan and others. According to this view, they were called "sacred" (ḥuruman) because the blood of the polytheists was made inviolable during them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then kill the polytheists⦆ — that is, those who have no covenant, "wherever you find them" (wajadtumuhum). Ibn 'Abbas said: "in the sacred territory (al-ḥill wa'l-ḥaram) and in the sacred months."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and seize them⦆ — that is, take them captive; al-akhidh means the captive. ﴿and besiege them⦆ — that is, confine them; al-ḥaṣr means confinement. Ibn 'Abbas said: "If they fortify themselves, then besiege them."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush⦆ — al-Akhfash said: that is, "on every place of ambush"; so he dropped "ʿalā" (on) and the verb operated directly. The poet said:

"We make the meat dear for the guests when raw, and cheapen it when the cooking-pots have boiled."

The meaning is "we make the price of meat high," so he omitted the "bi" (for), just as "ʿalā" was omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: "kulla marṣadin" is an adverbial of place (ẓarf), as in your saying "I went a way (madhhaban)"; in this verse you need say nothing beyond what is said of adverbs of place, such as "behind" (khalf) and "in front" (qiddam).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if they repent⦆ — that is, from their polytheism.

Concerning His saying: ﴿and establish the prayer and give the zakat⦆ there are two views.

One is that they acknowledge this. The second is that they actually do it.

Section

The scholars of abrogation (al-nasikh wa'l-mansukh) differed concerning this verse according to three views.

(p-399) One: the ruling concerning captives was that they had to be killed, then it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Then either grace after that or ransom⦆ [Muhammad: 4]. This is the view of al-Hasan and ʿAta' and others.

The second is the reverse: that the ruling concerning captives was that it was not permissible to kill them in cold blood (ṣabran); only grace or ransom was permitted, by His saying: ﴿Then either grace after that or ransom⦆. Then it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿then kill the polytheists⦆. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: the two verses are muhkam (not abrogated), and a captive who falls into the hands of the imam (ruler) is left to choose: if he wishes, he may show grace to him; if he wishes, he may ransom him; and if he wishes, he may kill him in cold blood — whichever course he judges to be in the interest of the Muslims. This is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd, and it is the position of the majority of jurists, and it is the view of Imam Ahmad.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 6:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾. The exegetes said: And if any one of the polytheists whom I have commanded you to kill seeks your safe-conduct (istiʾman), desiring to hear the Qur'an and to look into what he has been commanded and forbidden in it, then grant him protection, and then convey him to the place where he is safe.

As for His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾, there are two views.

One of them: the meaning is: that which We have commanded you concerning them, namely that they be informed and granted protection, is because of their ignorance of knowledge.

The second: that which We have commanded you concerning them, namely returning him to his place of safety if he refuses to believe, is because they are a people ignorant of the address of Allah.

[p. 400] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists﴾, meaning, there cannot be one for them, ﴿except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾. There are three opinions about them.

The first is that they are Banu Damra. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second is that they are Quraysh. This is also from Ibn Abbas. Qatada said: They are the polytheists of Quraysh with whom the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) made a covenant at the time of Hudaybiyya, but they broke it and backed the polytheists.

The third is that they are Khuza'a. This is the view of Mujahid. The scholars of the biographical histories (ahl al-sayr) mentioned that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made peace with Suhayl ibn Amr during the expedition of Hudaybiyya, the following was written between them: "This is what Muhammad ibn Abdullah and Suhayl ibn Amr have agreed upon. They agreed to suspend war for ten years, during which people will be safe and some will refrain from others, on the condition that there is no theft (islal) and no treachery (ighlal), and that between us there is a closed chest (ʿayba makfuwwa). Whoever wishes to enter the covenant and pact of Muhammad may do so, and whoever wishes to enter the covenant and pact of Quraysh may do so. Whoever of them comes to Muhammad without the permission of his guardian, he shall return him to him. Whoever of the companions of Muhammad comes to Quraysh, they shall not return him. Muhammad shall withdraw from us this year with his companions, and enter upon us next year with his companions, and he shall stay there three days, and he shall not enter upon us with weapons, except the weapons of a traveller, with the swords in their sheaths." Then Khuza'a rose and said: "We enter into the covenant and pact of Muhammad." Banu Bakr rose and said: "We enter into the covenant and pact of Quraysh." Then Quraysh aided Banu Bakr against Khuza'a with men and weapons, and they attacked Khuza'a by night, killing twenty men from them. Then Quraysh regretted what they had done, and they knew that this was a breach of the covenant and of the term that was between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). A group from Khuza'a went out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of what had befallen them. He went out to them, and that was the expedition of the Conquest.

Abu Ubayda said: al-islal means theft, and al-ighlal means treachery.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: His saying, "and that between us there is a closed chest," is a proverb. He meant that our peace is firm and secured, as if it were a tightly tied chest.

[p. 401] Some exegetes claimed that His saying, ﴿except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾, was abrogated (nusikha) by His saying: ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How, and if they gain the upper hand over you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: how can they have a covenant, and [how can it be kept] if they gain the upper hand over you? So that was omitted, because it had already been mentioned. The poet said:

﴿You told me that death is only in the villages, so how [can it be], and this is a hill and a well?﴾

That is: so how did he die, when he is not in a village? A similar line is the saying of al-Hutay'a:

﴿So how [can I be blamed], when I did not know them to have forsaken you, nor did they cut through your hide over a great one?﴾

That is: so how can you blame me for praising a people? The mention of that was dispensed with, because what had already occurred in the poem indicated what was implied. As for His saying yazhharu (yazhharu, "they gain the upper hand"), it means: they have power and they prevail.

In His saying ﴿they do not observe﴾ there are three opinions.

One: they do not preserve [it]. The second: they do not fear, said by al-Suddi. The third: they do not heed, said by Qutrub.

Regarding al-Ill (ill, a word meaning kinship or covenant) there are five opinions.

(p-402) One: it is kinship. This was transmitted by a group from Ibn Abbas, and it was said by al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and al-Farra', and they recited:

﴿Indeed, the slanderers are many if you obey them; they do not observe with us either kinship or covenant.﴾

Another said:

﴿By your life, indeed the ill of Quraysh is like the ill of the young camel of the ostrich's brood.﴾

The second: it is protection of a neighbour, said by al-Hasan.

The third: it is Allah, the Exalted, transmitted by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and 'Ikrimah also said it.

The fourth: it is the covenant, transmitted by Khasif from Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd and Abu 'Ubayda also said it.

The fifth: it is the alliance, said by Qatada. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, 'Ikrimah, Abu Raja' and Talha ibn Musarrif recited "iyalan" with a yā' after the hamza. Ibn al-Sameef and al-Jahdari recited "allan" with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the lam. Regarding what is meant by dhimma there are three opinions.

One: it is covenant, said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Dahhak and others.

The second: it is being bound by obligation toward one who has no covenant, said by Abu 'Ubayda, who recited:

﴿They do not observe with us either kinship or covenant.﴾

The third: it is safe-conduct, said by al-Yazidi, who cited his saying: "and their lowest man exerts himself on their dhimma (protection)."

(p-403) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions.

One: they please you with their mouths in fulfilling [promises], while their hearts refuse except treachery.

The second: they please you with their mouths in the pledge of faith, while their hearts refuse except polytheism.

The third: they please you with their mouths in obedience, while their hearts refuse except disobedience. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And most of them are defiant﴾. Ibn Abbas said: they depart from truthfulness, breaking the covenant.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 9–11:

His saying, Most High: ﴿They have exchanged the signs of Allah for a small price﴾. Concerning those referred to, there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Bedouin Arabs whom Abu Sufyan gathered for his food. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they are a people from among the Jews. This was said by Abu Salih. According to the first, the signs of Allah are His proofs (hujaj). According to the second, they are the signs of the Torah. The small price is what they obtained in exchange for the signs. Regarding describing it as small, there are two views.

The first: because it is unlawful (haram), and the unlawful is small. The second: because it is from the goods of this world, whose lasting is brief. Regarding His saying, ﴿So they averted [others] from His way﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: from His House, which occurred when they prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) at Hudaybiyyah from entering Makkah. The second: from His religion, by preventing people from it. The third: from obeying Him in fulfilling the covenant.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 9–11:

His saying, Most High: ﴿They have exchanged the signs of Allah for a small price﴾. Concerning those referred to, there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Bedouin Arabs whom Abu Sufyan gathered for his food. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they are a people from among the Jews. This was said by Abu Salih. According to the first, the signs of Allah are His proofs (hujaj). According to the second, they are the signs of the Torah. The small price is what they obtained in exchange for the signs. Regarding describing it as small, there are two views.

The first: because it is unlawful (haram), and the unlawful is small. The second: because it is from the goods of this world, whose lasting is brief. Regarding His saying, ﴿So they averted [others] from His way﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: from His House, which occurred when they prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) at Hudaybiyyah from entering Makkah. The second: from His religion, by preventing people from it. The third: from obeying Him in fulfilling the covenant.

(p-404) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they break their oaths﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Suhayl ibn 'Amr, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and the rest of the leaders of Quraysh who broke the covenant when they aided Banu Bakr against Khuza'a, the allies of the Messenger of Allah. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that he march against them to support Khuza'a, and they were the ones who had plotted to expel the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for *al-nakth* (نَكْث), its meaning is *al-naqd* (النَّقْض), breaking. *Al-iman* (الإيمان) here means the covenants. *Al-ta'n fi al-din* (الطَّعْن في الدِّين), attacking the religion, means to find fault with it. This requires the killing of the *dhimmi* (الذِّمِّيّ, a non-Muslim living under the protection of the Muslim state) if he attacks Islam, because he was bound by the obligation not to attack it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read *a'immah* (أئِمَّة) with both hamzas pronounced in full. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read it with the first hamza pronounced in full and the second softened. *Qira'at* (القراءات, the canonical recitations) differ in this way. The meaning of *a'immat al-kufr* (أئِمَّةَ الكُفْرِ) is the heads and commanders of the polytheists. ﴿Indeed, they have no oaths﴾, that is, no valid covenants for them. This is according to the reading of those who open the alif (فتح الألف) in *aymanun* (أيْمانَ), and they are the majority. Ibn 'Amir read *la iman lahum* (لا إيمانَ لَهُمْ) with a kasra, and al-Zajjaj mentioned two possible meanings for it.

One is that it describes them with disbelief and negates faith from them. The second is that it means they have no safe-conduct (لا أمانَ لَهم). You say *amantuhu iman* (آمَنْتُهُ إيمانًا), and the meaning is: your safe-conduct for them has become void by their breaking of it.

(p-405) Regarding Allah's saying ﴿so that they may desist﴾, there are two opinions. One is that it refers to desisting from polytheism. The second is that it refers to desisting from breaking covenants.

Regarding *la'alla* (لَعَلَّ, "perhaps"), there are two opinions. One is that it has the sense of hope (التَّرَجِّي), meaning that cessation is hoped for from them; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The second is that it has the sense of *kay* (كَيْ, "in order that"); this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: This is in the form of reproach, and its meaning is an urging to fight them. The exegetes said: This was revealed concerning the breach by the Quraysh of the covenant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he had made with them at al-Hudaybiyyah, when they aided [Banu Bakr] against Khuza'ah.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And they plotted to expel the Messenger﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: they were Abu Sufyan and a group of the Quraysh, who were among those who plotted to expel the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah.

The second: they were a people of the Jews, who betrayed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), broke his covenant, and plotted with the hypocrites to help expel him from Madinah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they began against you first time﴾ has two opinions.

The first: they began against you by aiding their allies against you. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: [they began] with fighting on the day of Badr. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-406) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you fear them?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Do you fear that some harm will befall you from fighting them? Then the harm of the punishment of Allah is more deserving of being feared, if you truly believe in His punishment and His reward.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He will heal the breasts of a believing people﴾ Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: It means Khuza'ah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And remove the rage of their hearts﴾ meaning their distress and grief over it, through the aid of the Quraysh to Banu Bakr against them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: It is a new clause, and not an answer to "fight them." Concerning who is meant by it there are two opinions.

The first: the sons of Khuza'ah, meaning: Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills from the sons of Khuza'ah. This was said by Ikrimah.

The second: it is general concerning the polytheists, as He turned in forgiveness to Abu Sufyan, Ikrimah, and Suhayl. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the intentions of the believers, All-Wise﴾ in what He decrees.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or did you think that you would be left alone﴾, concerning those addressed by this, there are two opinions.

The first: they are the believers, who were addressed with this when fighting was difficult for some of them. This was said by most scholars.

The second: they are a group of the hypocrites who used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out with him to jihad, making excuses. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The letter mim (mim in the interrogative, "am") entered the interrogation because it is an interrogation interjected into the middle of the speech, so it was added to distinguish it from the initiating interrogation. Al-Farra' said: If it were intended as an initiating question, it would be either with the alif (hamza of interrogation) or with "hal" (is/does). The meaning of the speech: that you would be left without a test by which the truthful is distinguished from the liar. ﴿And Allah has not yet known﴾, i.e., you have not striven, so that Allah would know the existence of that from you; although He already knew that unseen, He wanted to make manifest what was known so that He would reward for the deed.

As for al-Waliyjah (the intimate, inner circle), Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the close associate from among non-Muslims, that is, a man from among the Muslims takes an intimate from among the polytheists, a companion and a loving friend. Its root is from al-wulouj (entering). Abu Ubayda said: Everything you insert into something that is not part of it is a waliyjah, and a man who is among a people while not being of them is a waliyjah among them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 17–18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "masjid Allah" (mosque of Allah) in the singular (al-tawhid), and "innama ya'muru masajid Allah" (it is only those who maintain the mosques of Allah) in the plural (al-jam'). ʿAsim, Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited both in the plural (al-jam') form. The occasion of its revelation was that a group of the leaders of Quraysh were taken captive on the Day of Badr, among them al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib. Some of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approached them and reproached them for polytheism, and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib began rebuking al-ʿAbbas for fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and for severing the ties of kinship. Al-ʿAbbas said: "What is the matter with you, that you mention our faults and conceal our virtues?" They said: "Do you have any virtues?" They said: "Yes, indeed, we are better than you in reward: we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we serve the Ka'bah with its covering, we give drink to the pilgrims, and we ransom the captive." Then this verse was revealed. This was related by Muqatil concerning a group.

Regarding the meaning of "maintenance" (al-ʿimarah), there are two opinions.

The first: entering it and sitting in it. The second: building it and repairing it. Both are forbidden to the disbeliever. The meaning of His saying ﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ is: it is obligatory upon the Muslims to prevent them from that. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying "witnessing against themselves" (shahidayn) is a circumstantial clause (hal). The meaning is: their maintenance of it was not valid while they acknowledged disbelief. ﴿Those—their deeds have become worthless﴾, because their disbelief removed its reward.

If it is said: how can they bear witness against themselves with disbelief while they believe they are upon the truth? In answer to this there are three responses.

The first: it is the statement of the Jew, "I am a Jew," and the statement of the Christian, "I am a Christian." This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: they established disbelief against themselves by their turning away from the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is a truth not hidden from one who discerns, so they were in the position of one who testifies against himself.

The third: they believed in prophets who had testified to Muhammad (ﷺ) with confirmation and urged following him; when they believed in those prophets and denied him, they indicated their disbelief, and this took the place of testimony against themselves regarding disbelief, because testimony is clarification and manifestation. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two.

If it is said: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Only those who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ without mentioning the Messenger, while faith is not complete without him? The answer: there is in it an indication of the Messenger, by His saying ﴿and establishes prayer﴾, meaning the prayer which the Messenger brought. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

If it is said: "perhaps" (ʿasa) indicates expectation, and the doer of these qualities is undoubtedly guided. The answer: "ʿasa" (perhaps) from Allah is binding. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

If it is said: one may maintain the mosques of Allah without possessing these qualities. The answer: the intended meaning is that whoever has these described qualities is among the people of its maintenance; it is not meant that whoever maintains it has these qualities.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verses 19–22:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾ There are six reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: Muslim related it in his Sahih from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: "I was near the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when a man said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after (accepting) Islam except giving water to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after (accepting) Islam except building up the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Jihad in the way of Allah is better than what you have said.' Umar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices near the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it is Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter and ask the Messenger of Allah concerning what you disagree about.' So this verse was revealed."

The second: that al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib said on the day of Badr: "If you have preceded us in Islam, emigration and jihad, then we used to build up the Sacred Mosque, give water to the pilgrims, and free the captives." So this verse was revealed. Ali ibn Abi Talhah related it from Ibn Abbas.

The third: the polytheists said: "Maintaining the House of Allah, the Sacred, and attending to the watering (of pilgrims) is better than one who believes and strives in jihad." They used to boast of the Sacred Precinct because they were its people. So this verse was revealed. Atiyyah al-Awfi related it from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that Ali, al-Abbas and Talhah, meaning the custodian of the Ka'bah, boasted. Talhah said: "I am the master of the House; its key is in my hand, and if I wished I could spend the night in it." Al-Abbas said: "I am the master of the watering, and the one in charge of it; and if I wished I could spend the night in the mosque." Ali said: "I do not know what you are saying. I prayed six months before the people, and I am the master of jihad." So this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and al-Qurazi.

The fifth: when they were commanded to emigrate, al-Abbas said: "I give water to the pilgrims," and Talhah said: "I am the keeper of the Ka'bah, so we will not emigrate." So this verse and the one after it were revealed. This was said by Mujahid. Thus Mujahid mentioned it, but the correct name is Uthman ibn Talhah, because this Talhah did not accept Islam.

The sixth: that Ali said to al-Abbas: "Will you not join the Prophet ﷺ?" He said: "Am I not in a better position than emigration? Am I not giving water to the pilgrims of the House of Allah and building up the Sacred Mosque?" So this verse and the one after it were revealed. This was said by al-Murrah al-Hamdani and Ibn Sirin.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "Do you consider the people who give water to the pilgrims and the people who build up the Sacred Mosque to be like one who believes in Allah?" He omitted the genitive (mudaf) and put the noun in the genitive position (mudaf ilayhi) in its place.

Al-Hasan said: "They used to make nabidh from raisins, and they would give the pilgrims drink during the season." Ibn Abbas said: "Building up the mosque means fumigating it with incense and perfuming it." Allah informed that these deeds of theirs do not benefit them along with polytheism, and He called them wrongdoers because of their polytheism.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿greater in rank﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning: greater in rank than others. "The successful" (al-fa'iz) is the one who attains his wish of good. As for "bliss" (al-na'im), it is the pleasant life, and "lasting" (al-muqim) means enduring.

Umar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices near the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it is Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter and ask the Messenger of Allah concerning what you disagree about.' So this verse was revealed."

The second: that al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib said on the day of Badr: "If you have preceded us in Islam, emigration and jihad, then we used to build up the Sacred Mosque, give water to the pilgrims, and free the captives." So this verse was revealed. Ali ibn Abi Talhah related it from Ibn Abbas.

The third: the polytheists said: "Maintaining the House of Allah, the Sacred, and attending to the watering (of pilgrims) is better than one who believes and strives in jihad." They used to boast of the Sacred Precinct because they were its people. So this verse was revealed. Atiyyah al-Awfi related it from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that Ali, al-Abbas and Talhah, meaning the custodian of the Ka'bah, boasted. Talhah said: "I am the master of the House; its key is in my hand, and if I wished I could spend the night in it." Al-Abbas said: "I am the master of the watering, and the one in charge of it; and if I wished I could spend the night in the mosque." Ali said: "I do not know what you are saying. I prayed six months before the people, and I am the master of jihad." So this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and al-Qurazi.

The fifth: when they were commanded to emigrate, al-Abbas said: "I give water to the pilgrims," and Talhah said: "I am the keeper of the Ka'bah, so we will not emigrate." So this verse and the one after it were revealed. This was said by Mujahid. Thus Mujahid mentioned it, but the correct name is Uthman ibn Talhah, because this Talhah did not accept Islam.

The sixth: that Ali said to al-Abbas: "Will you not join the Prophet ﷺ?" He said: "Am I not in a better position than emigration? Am I not giving water to the pilgrims of the House of Allah and building up the Sacred Mosque?" So this verse and the one after it were revealed. This was said by al-Murrah al-Hamdani and Ibn Sirin.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "Do you consider the people who give water to the pilgrims and the people who build up the Sacred Mosque to be like one who believes in Allah?" He omitted the genitive (mudaf) and put the noun in the genitive position (mudaf ilayhi) in its place.

Al-Hasan said: "They used to make nabidh from raisins, and they would give the pilgrims drink during the season." Ibn Abbas said: "Building up the mosque means fumigating it with incense and perfuming it." Allah informed that these deeds of theirs do not benefit them along with polytheism, and He called them wrongdoers because of their polytheism.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿greater in rank﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning: greater in rank than others. "The successful" (al-fa'iz) is the one who attains his wish of good. As for "bliss" (al-na'im), it is the pleasant life, and "lasting" (al-muqim) means enduring.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are five opinions.

The first: When the Muslims were commanded to emigrate (hijrah), a man would say to his family, "We have been commanded to emigrate." Some of them hastened to do so, while others were held back by their dependents and wives, who would say, "We implore you by God not to leave us for nothing." His heart would soften and he would sit with them, and then this verse was revealed. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: When God commanded the believers to emigrate, the Muslims said, "O Prophet of God, if we withdraw from those who oppose us in religion, we will cut off our fathers and our clans, our trade will be lost, and our homes will be ruined." Then this verse was revealed. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The third: When al-Abbas said, "I will give water to the pilgrims," and Talhah said, "I will keep the Ka'bah," and so they did not emigrate, this verse and the one before it were revealed. This is the saying of Qatadah, and we have mentioned it from Mujahid.

The fourth: A group of people apostatized from Islam and joined Mecca, so God forbade alliance with them and revealed this verse. This was related by Muqatil.

The fifth: "When the Prophet ﷺ commanded the people to wage jihad to support Khuza'ah against Quraysh, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said, 'O Messenger of God, should we assist them against our own people?' Then this verse was revealed." This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 24:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: If your fathers, and your sons...﴾ [the verse], concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first is that it was revealed concerning those who remained behind in Makkah with their dependents and did not emigrate. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib came to Makkah and said to a people: "Will you not emigrate?" They said: "We will remain with our brothers, our clans, and our dwellings." So this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Sirin.

The third is that when the preceding verse was revealed, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, if we withdraw from those who oppose us in the religion, we will cut off our fathers and our clan, our trade will perish, and our homes will be ruined." So this verse was revealed. Some of the exegetes mentioned this as the occasion for this verse, while some of them mentioned it for the first verse, as we related from Ibn 'Abbas.

As for ﴿al-'ashirah﴾ (the clan), it refers to the closest relatives. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim the reading ﴿wa-'asheeratukum﴾ (and your clans) in the plural. Abu 'Ali said: its reasoning is that each of the addressees has a clan, so when you pluralize you say "'asheeratukum." The argument of those who used the singular is that ﴿al-'ashirah﴾ is applied to a collective, so it is sufficient without pluralizing it. Al-Akhfash said: the Arabs hardly ever pluralize ﴿'asheerah﴾ as ﴿'asheerat﴾; rather they pluralize it as ﴿'asha'ir﴾. The word ﴿iqtiraf﴾ (acquisition, earning) means ﴿iktisab﴾ (gaining). And ﴿tarabbus﴾ (waiting) means ﴿intizar﴾ (expecting).

Regarding His saying: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them is that it is the conquest of Makkah. This was said by Mujahid and most of the scholars. The meaning of the verse is: if your dwelling among your families, the wealth you have acquired, ﴿and a commerce you fear will decline﴾ due to your leaving your land, ﴿and dwellings you prefer over Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause﴾ over emigration, then remain without reward until Makkah is conquered, whereupon the obligation of emigration falls away.

The second is that it is the punishment. This was said by al-Hasan.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 9, verse 25:**

(p-414) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah has given you victory on many battlefields﴾, meaning: in many places. Al-Farra' said: Every plural in which there is an alif preceded by two letters and followed by two letters is not declined (does not take tanwin), such as *sawami'* and *masajid*. *Hunayn* was declined because it is the name of a masculine thing. It is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if. When you name a water, valley or mountain with a masculine name that has no other cause for non-declension, you decline it, such as *Hunayn*, *Badr*, *Hira'*, *Thabir* and *Dabiq*. The meaning of the verse is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed them that they were only victorious by the help of Allah, not by their numbers. Regarding their number on the day of Hunayn, there are four opinions.

The first is that they were sixteen thousand. This was related by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is ten thousand. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third is that they were twelve thousand. This was said by Qatada, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi.

The fourth is eleven thousand and five hundred. This was said by Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: Salama ibn Salama ibn Waqsh said on that day, marvelling at the multitude of people: "We will not be defeated today from paucity." This displeased the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were left to the words of that man. That is His saying: ﴿When your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing﴾. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: The one who said that was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ibn Jarir related that the one who said it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: rather, al-'Abbas. And it was said: a man from Bakr.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the earth became constricted for you despite its vastness﴾, meaning: despite its breadth. Al-Farra' said: The *ba'* here has the function of *fi*, as when you say: "The earth became constricted for you in its breadth and with its breadth."

**Reference to the story**

The people of knowledge of the biography (*al-Sira*) said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, the nobles of Hawazin and Thaqif conspired against him. They came and camped at Awtas and resolved to march against him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to them, and when they met, their great numbers pleased them, and they were routed."

Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "When we charged against them, they fled, and we fell upon the spoils. Then they turned back with arrows, and the Muslims fled away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Some say: (p-415) a group of his Companions remained with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that day, including Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, al-'Abbas, and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith.

Some say: none remained with him except al-'Abbas and Abu Sufyan. The Prophet began saying to al-'Abbas: "Call out, O company of the Ansar, O companions of the tree (*al-Samurah*), O companions of Surah al-Baqarah!" So he called out, and he had a loud voice. They came back like camels when they yearn for their young, saying: "Here we are, at your service!" The Prophet (ﷺ) looked at their fighting and said: "Now the furnace has grown hot." Then he said: "I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib." Then he said to al-'Abbas: "Hand me the pebbles." So he handed them to him, and he said: "May the faces be disfigured," and threw them, and said: "Flee, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!" So Allah cast terror into their hearts, and they fled. It was also said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took a handful of dust, threw it at them, and they fled. They used to say: "None of us remained except that his eyes were filled with the dust."

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿ثُمَّ أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ سَكِينَتَهُ﴾ أيْ: بَعْدَ الهَزِيمَةِ. قالَ أبُو عُبَيْدَةَ: هي فَعِيلَةٌ مِنَ السُّكُونِ، وأنْشَدَ:(p-٤١٦)

؎ لِلَّهِ قَبْرُ غالَها ماذا يُجِنُّ لَقَدْ أجَنَّ سَكِينَةً ووَقارًا

By God, a grave that has taken her—what does it conceal? It has indeed concealed tranquility and dignity.

وَكَذَلِكَ قالَ المُفَسِّرُونَ: الأمْنُ والطُّمَأْنِينَةُ.

Likewise the exegetes (mufassirun) said: it is security and peace of heart.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَأنْزَلَ جُنُودًا لَمْ تَرَوْها﴾ قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ: يَعْنِي المَلائِكَةَ. وفي عَدَدِهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ ثَلاثَةُ أقْوالٍ.

﴿And He sent down hosts you did not see﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the angels. Regarding their number on that day, there are three opinions.

أحَدُها: سِتَّةَ عَشَرَ ألْفًا، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ. والثّانِي: خَمْسَةُ آَلافٍ، قالَهُ سَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ. والثّالِثُ: ثَمانِيَةٌ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ، يَعْنِي ثَمانِيَةُ آَلافٍ. وهَلْ قاتَلَتِ المَلائِكَةُ يَوْمَئِذٍ، أمْ لا؟ فِيهِ قَوْلانِ.

The first: sixteen thousand, said by al-Hasan. The second: five thousand, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The third: eight, said by Mujahid, meaning eight thousand. As to whether the angels fought on that day or not, there are two opinions.

وَفِي قَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَعَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ أرْبَعَةُ أقْوالٍ.

Regarding His saying, ﴿and He punished those who disbelieved﴾, there are four opinions.

أحَدُها: بِالقَتْلِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ، والسُّدِّيُّ. والثّانِي: بِالقَتْلِ والهَزِيمَةِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ أبْزى، ومُقاتِلٌ. والثّالِثُ: بِالخَوْفِ والحَذَرِ، ذَكَرَهُ الماوَرْدِيُّ. والرّابِعُ: بِالقَتْلِ، والأسْرِ، وسَبْيِ الأوْلادِ، وأخْذِ الأمْوالِ، ذَكَرَهُ بَعْضُ ناقِلِي التَّفْسِيرِ.

The first: by killing, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. The second: by killing and defeat, said by Ibn Abza and Muqatil. The third: by fear and dread, mentioned by al-Mawardi. The fourth: by killing, capture, taking of children as captives, and seizing of property, mentioned by some of the transmitters of tafsir (exegesis).

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلى مِن يَشاءُ﴾ أيْ: يُوَفِّقُهُ لَلتَّوْبَةِ مِنَ الشِّرْكِ.

﴿Then God accepts repentance after that from whom He wills﴾: that is, He grants him success in repenting from shirk (associating partners with God).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 28:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is "filth" (qadhar). Al-Zajjaj said: "najis" is said of everything that is considered repugnant. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs hardly say "najas" except that before it is "rijs" (abomination); when they use it alone, they say "najas."

(p-417) Regarding the intended meaning of their being "najas," there are three opinions.

The first: they are unclean in their bodies, like the dog and the pig. Al-Mawardi related this from al-Hasan and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz. Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan that he said: "Whoever shakes hands with them should perform wudu'."

The second: they are like unclean things because they abandon what is obligatory upon them of ghusl from janabah, even if their bodies are not unclean. This was said by Qatada.

The third: since it is incumbent upon us to avoid them, as unclean things are avoided, they become, by the ruling of avoidance, like unclean things. This is the view of the majority, and it is the sound one.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram﴾. The people of tafsir said: it means the entire Haram. (After this year of theirs) — which is the ninth year of the Hijra, the year in which Abu Bakr performed Hajj, and Bara'a was recited. Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, took the apparent meaning of the verse, that it is forbidden for them to enter the Haram; this is also the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Narrations from him differed concerning their entering mosques other than al-Masjid al-Haram. It is related from him that they are also prohibited, except for a need, as with the Haram; this is the view of Malik. It is also related from him that it is permissible, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: it is permissible for them to enter al-Masjid al-Haram and all other mosques.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: "ā'ilatan." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs﴾ was revealed, it grieved the Muslims, and they said: "Who will bring us our food?" They used to come to them with trade, so the verse was revealed: ﴿And if you fear poverty...﴾, the verse. Al-Akhfash said: "al-'ayla" means poverty. It is said: "'ala ya'ilu 'aylatan" when one becomes poor, and "a'ala ita'latan fa-huwa yu'ilu" when one becomes the head of a family. Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-'ayla" here is a verbal noun of "'ala fulan," when he became poor, and he recited:

"The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor."

Regarding His saying "wa-in" (and if), the commentators have two views.

One: it is conditional, and this is the more apparent.

The second: it means "wa-idh" (and when), said by 'Amr ibn Fa'id. They said: the Muslims only feared poverty because the polytheists used to bring their goods to them and come with food and other things.

Regarding His saying: ﴿Then Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills﴾, there are three opinions.

One: that He sent rain upon them when the polytheists cut off from them, so their goodness increased. This was said by 'Ikrima.

The second: that He enriched them through the jizya taken from the People of the Book. This was said by Qatada and al-Dahhak.

The third: that the people of Najd, Jarash, and Sana'a embraced Islam, and they carried food to Makka on the backs of animals, so Allah enriched them with it. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Knowing of what sets right your affairs, (Wise) in what He has decreed concerning the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 29:

(p-419) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾. The exegetes said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: they do not believe in Allah with the faith of those who affirm His oneness (muwahhidun), because they acknowledged that He is their Creator and that He has a son; and likewise their belief in the Resurrection, since they do not affirm that the people of Paradise eat and drink. Al-Mawardi said: their affirmation of the Last Day necessitates affirming its rights, and they do not affirm these, so they are like one who does not affirm it at all.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: meaning wine and swine.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor do they follow the religion of truth﴾. Concerning "the truth" there are two opinions.

One of them: it is a name of Allah, so the meaning is: the religion of Allah. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: it is an attribute of the religion, and the meaning is: nor do they follow the true religion; so the noun is idafa'd to the attribute. Concerning the meaning of "yadinuna" (they follow/submit to) there are two opinions.

(p-420) One of them: it has the meaning of obedience, and the meaning is: they do not obey Allah with true obedience. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda. The second: it derives from "dana", as in "the man yadinu kadha" (he binds himself to such and such), meaning: when he commits himself to it. Then concerning the sense of the whole sentence there are two opinions.

One of them: the meaning is: they do not enter the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), because it abrogates what came before it (naskh).

The second: they do not act upon what is in the Torah concerning following Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Until they give the jizyah﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: the jizyah is the tribute imposed upon them; it was named jizyah because it is a settlement of what is owed by them, taken from their saying "jazaa yajzee" (it suffices/settles), when it means "qada" (to discharge); and from it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿No soul will avail another soul anything﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:48], and His saying "wa la tajzee 'an ahadin ba'dak" (and it will not avail anyone after you). Concerning His saying: ("an yadin" – "by hand" / "from a position of strength"), there are six opinions.

One of them: "from subjugation," said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: from subjugation and humiliation.

The second: it is the immediate payment, said by Sharik and Uthman ibn Muqsim.

The third: it is giving by one who initiates the giving, not giving by one who repays in kind, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The fourth: the meaning is: from acknowledgment by the Muslims that their hands are above their hands.

The fifth: from a favour bestowed upon them by it, since accepting the jizyah from them is a favour to them; both of these were related by al-Zajjaj.

The sixth: they pay it with their own hands, and do not send it through their envoys; mentioned by al-Mawardi.

(p-421) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿While they are humbled (sagharun)﴾. The saghir is the humiliated, the abject.

Concerning the act they are required to perform that necessitates their humiliation there are five opinions.

One of them: that they walk with it bound by the collar (mulabbibin), related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that they should not be praised for their giving, said by Salman al-Farisi. The third: that they stand while the collector sits, said by Ikrimah. The fourth: that the paying of the jizyah itself is the humiliation. The fifth: that the enforcement of the rulings of Islam upon them is the humiliation.

Section

There is disagreement about who among the disbelievers is subject to the jizyah. The well-known position from Ahmad is that it is accepted only from the Jews, the Christians and the Magians, and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i. Al-Hasan ibn Thawab related from Ahmad that whoever is taken captive from the people of other religions, among the Arabs and the non-Arabs, the Arabs are either to embrace Islam or face the sword, and those others are either to embrace Islam or pay the jizyah; the apparent meaning of this is that the jizyah is taken from all, except only the idol-worshippers among the Arabs, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa and Malik.

Section

As for the description of those from whom the jizyah is taken, they are the people of fighting. As for the chronically ill, the blind, the paralysed, the aged decrepit, women, children, and the monk who does not mix with people, the jizyah is not taken from them.

(p-422) Section

As for its amount, our companions said: upon the wealthy, forty-eight dirhams; upon the middle-class, twenty-four; and upon the poor who is able to work, twelve; and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. Malik's view: upon the people of gold, four dinars, and upon the people of silver, forty dirhams, and rich and poor alike are equal in this. Al-Shafi'i said: upon the rich and the poor alike, one dinar. And is it permissible to increase or decrease what is taken from them? Al-Athram related from Ahmad that it may be increased or decreased according to their capacity; the apparent meaning of this is that it is according to the ruler's judgment and opinion. Ya'qub ibn Bakhtan related that it is not permissible for the ruler to decrease from this, but he may increase it.

Section

The time when the jizyah becomes due is the end of the year, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: it becomes due at the beginning of the year. As for when one year passes into another, does the jizyah of the past year fall away? According to us, it does not fall away. Abu Hanifa said: it falls away. As for when one of them embraces Islam, it falls away by Islam. As for if he dies, Ibn Hamid used to say: it does not fall away. And al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: it is possible that it falls away.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 30–31:

(p-423) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Jews say: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah."﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir and Hamzah read "ʿUzayru ibnu Allah" without tanwin (nunation). ʿAsim, al-Kisa'i, Yaʿqub and ʿAbd al-Warith on the authority of Abu ʿAmr read it with tanwin. Makki ibn Abi Talib said: whoever reads ʿUzayran with tanwin makes it nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with "ibn" as its predicate (khabar). The deletion of the tanwin on "ʿUzayr" in this case is not good, because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). The alif of "ibn" is not dropped in the script, and the tanwin is vowelled with a kasra because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters. Whoever does not read ʿUzayran with tanwin also makes it the subject, with "ibn" as its attribute (sifah); the tanwin is then deleted on this reading for lightness (istikhfaf) because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters, and because the attribute together with the thing described is like one thing. The alif of "ibn" is dropped in the script, and the predicate is implied, its estimate being: "ʿUzayr, the son of Allah, is our prophet and our companion."

The occasion of revelation was that Sallam ibn Mushkim, Nu'man ibn Awfa, Shas ibn Qays and Malik ibn al-Sayf came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "How can we follow you when you have abandoned our qibla, and you do not claim that ʿUzayr is the son of Allah?" So this verse was revealed. This was reported by Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Jurayj said that the one who said this was Finhas.

As for ʿUzayr, our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: it is a non-Arabic name that has been Arabized, and even if it matches an Arabic word in form, it is Hebrew; so I read it under him. Makki ibn Abi Talib said: according to all the grammarians, ʿUzayr is Arabic, derived from the saying "yuʿazziruhu" (they honour him).

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they only said this because, when they had acted contrary to the truth, Allah made them forget the Torah and removed it from their breasts. ʿUzayr then called upon Allah, the Exalted, and what had been removed from their breasts returned to him, and a light descended from the sky and entered his body. He then informed his people, saying: "Allah has given me the Torah." They said: "He was only given it because he is the son of Allah."

In another report from Ibn ʿAbbas: when Bukhtnassar (p-424) prevailed over the Children of Israel, destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, and killed those who recited the Torah, ʿUzayr was a boy and was spared. When ʿUzayr died in Babylon and remained dead for a hundred years, Allah, the Exalted, raised him up to the Children of Israel. He said: "I am ʿUzayr." They denied him and said: "Our fathers have related to us that ʿUzayr died in Babylon. If you are ʿUzayr, dictate the Torah to us." So he wrote it out for them, and they said: "This is the son of Allah."

Regarding those who said this about ʿUzayr there are three views.

The first: they were all the Children of Israel, reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: a group of their predecessors, said by al-Mawardi. The third: a group who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and concerning them there are two views.

One of them: Finhas alone, and we have mentioned this from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: those we mentioned at the beginning of the verse, from Ibn ʿAbbas.

If it is asked: if it was the saying of some of them, why is it attributed to all of them? There are two answers to this.

One: applying a collective term to an individual is well known in the language; the Arabs say, "I came from Basra on mules," even though he rode only one mule.

Two: whoever did not say it did not deny it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Christians say: "The Messiah is the son of Allah."﴾ Concerning the reason for their saying this there are two views.

One: because he was born without a father.

Two: because he raised the dead and healed the blind and the leper; we have explained this meaning in (al-Ma'idah: 110).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is their saying with their mouths.﴾ If someone says: this is known, so what is its benefit? The answer: the meaning is that it is a saying by the mouth alone, with no evidence or proof in it, and no sound meaning beneath it; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: "Yudahun" (they imitate). The majority read it without hamza. ʿAsim read (p-425) "yudahi'un" with hamza. Tha'lab said: no one else followed ʿAsim in the hamza. al-Farra' said: it is a dialect. al-Zajjaj said: "yudahun" means they resemble the saying of those who came before them among their disbelievers; they only said it following their predecessors. The root meaning of mudahah in the language is resemblance; the more common usage drops the hamza; its derivation is from their saying: "imra'ah dahya'" (a woman with no breasts), who has no breast growing. It was also said: she is one who does not menstruate, and the meaning is that she has come to resemble men. Ibn al-Anbari said: one says "dahayta" and "dahata'ta" when you make a comparison.

Regarding "those who disbelieved" here there are three views.

One: they are idolaters, and the meaning is that those said: the angels are the daughters of Allah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are the Jews, and the meaning is that the Christians, in their saying "The Messiah is the son of Allah," resembled the Jews in their saying "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah"; this was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The third: they are their forefathers, whom they followed in their sayings by imitation (taqlid); this was said by al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿May Allah destroy them﴾ there are three views.

One: its meaning is "May Allah curse them," said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: "May Allah kill them," said by Abu ʿUbaydah. The third: "May Allah oppose them," mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ That is: from where are they turned away from the truth?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They took their rabbis﴾ The meaning of "rabbis" (ahbar) and "monks" (ruhban) has already been discussed in (al-Ma'idah: 44). It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about this verse and said: "As for them, they did not worship them, but when they made something lawful for them they considered it lawful, and when they made something unlawful for them they considered it unlawful." According to this meaning, they treated them as lords, even though they did not say that they were lords.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: they took him as a lord.
