Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they want to extinguish the religion of Allah by their denial, meaning: they deny it and turn away from it, wishing thereby to nullify it. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the light of Allah is the Qur'an and Islam. As for restricting this to the mouths, that is because of what we mentioned in the verse before it. It has also been said: Allah, exalted is He, never mentions a saying coupled with the mouths and tongues except that it is falsehood.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾. Al-Farra' said: "illa" (except) enters here because refusing (ʾibaʾ) carries a element of negation. Do you not see that "abaytu" (I refused) is like your saying "lam afʿal" (I did not do) and "wa la afʿal" (nor do I do), so it is as if it were in the position of your saying: "ma dhahaba illa Zayd" (none went except Zayd). The poet said:

﻿Is there for me a mother other than her, if I leave her? Allah refuses except that I be to her a son.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: and Allah refuses everything except the perfecting of His light. Muqatil said: "yatimmu nurahu" means: He makes His religion manifest.

(p-427) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿with guidance﴾, and on this there are three opinions.

The first is that it is monotheism (tawhid). The second is the Qur'an. The third is the explanation of the obligatory duties (al-fara'id). As for "the religion of truth," it is Islam. Regarding His saying, ﴿that He may make it prevail﴾, there are two views.

The first is that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the meaning is: that He may teach him all the laws of the religion, so that nothing of them is hidden from him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that the pronoun refers to the religion. Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are two views.

The first is that He may make this religion prevail over all the other creeds (milal). And when will that happen? (p-428) On this there are two views. The first is at the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him), for every people of every religion will follow him, the creeds will become one, and no people of any religion will remain except that they either enter Islam or pay the jizya. This was said by Abu Hurayra and al-Dahhak. The second is that it will happen at the emergence of the Mahdi. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second view is that the prevailing of the religion is only through clear proofs, even if people do not enter it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 34:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, many of the rabbis﴾. The rabbis (al-ahbar) are from among the Jews, and the monks (al-ruhban) are from among the Christians. Regarding "falsehood" (al-batil) there are four opinions.

The first: that it is injustice (al-zulm), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: bribery in judgment (al-rishā fi al-hukm), said by al-Hasan. The third: lying (al-kadhib), said by Abu Sulayman. The fourth: taking it from a forbidden source, said by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. The intended meaning is the taking of wealth, and only "consuming" (al-akl) is mentioned because it is the main purpose of wealth.

Regarding the intended meaning of "the way of Allah" (sabil Allah) here, there are two opinions.

One of them: faith in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second: that it is the truth and the judgment.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾. They differed regarding who was revealed concerning them, in three opinions.

The first: that it was revealed in general about the People of the Book and the Muslims, said by Abu Dharr and al-Dahhak.

The second: that it is specific to the People of the Book, said by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan.

The third: that it is about the Muslims, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

Regarding the hoard upon which this threat falls, there are three opinions.

The first: that it is whatever its zakat has not been paid. Ibn 'Umar said: "Every wealth whose zakat has been paid, even if it is under seven earths, is not a hoard; and every wealth whose zakat has not been paid is a hoard, even if it is apparent on the surface of the earth." The majority went to this meaning. Based on this, the meaning of "spending" (al-infaq) is the payment of zakat.

The second: that it is what exceeds four thousand. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "Four thousand is provision (nafaqa), and whatever is above it is a hoard."

The third: what is left over beyond need, and it was obligatory upon them to pay that out at the beginning of Islam, then it was abrogated (nusikha) by zakat.

If it is said: how did He say "they spend it" (yunfiquna-ha) when He mentioned two things? To this there are two answers.

One of them: the meaning returns to the hoards and the wealth.

The second: that it returns to the silver, and the gold is omitted because it is included in the silver. The poet said:

﴿We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, though opinions differ﴾

He means: we are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have. Al-Zajjaj mentioned both sayings.

Al-Farra' said: if you wish, you may suffice with one of the two mentioned, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever earns a sin or an offense and then throws it upon an innocent one﴾ [al-Nisa': 112], and His saying: ﴿And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed toward it﴾. And he recited:

﴿Indeed I have guaranteed for whoever came to me what he committed, and refused, and I was not a betrayer﴾

He did not say "treacherous ones" (ghadurin), but suffices with the singular because the meaning agrees. Abu 'Ubayda said: when the Arabs join two together, they shorten, reporting about one of them, relying on that and for affirmation, since the listener knows that the other has shared with him and entered into that report. And he recited:

﴿Whoever has his dwelling in Medina, then I and Qayyar are strangers therein﴾

The accusative in "Qayyar" is better, though the nominative is also possible. Hassan ibn Thabit said:

﴿The bloom of youth and the black hair, as long as it is not disobeyed, was madness﴾

And he did not say "yu'asiya" (they disobey).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 35:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day it will be heated in the fire of Hell﴾ — i.e., upon the wealth. Ibn Mas'ud said: "By Allah, there is no man who is branded with a hoard whereby a dinar is placed upon a dinar or a dirham upon a dirham; rather, his skin is widened and each dinar and dirham is placed upon its own spot."

And Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is a serpent that coils around his two sides and his forehead, and it says: 'I am your wealth which you withheld.'"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿This is what you hoarded﴾ — there is an omitted element in it, its estimate being: "And it will be said to them, 'This is what you hoarded for yourselves.'" ﴿So taste what you used to hoard⌋ — i.e., the punishment of that.

If it is said: Why did He single out the foreheads, sides and backs from the rest of the body?

The answer: These places are hollow, so the heat reaches their insides, unlike the hand and the foot. Abu Dharr used to say: "Give the hoarders the good news of a branding on the foreheads, a branding on the sides, and a branding on the backs, until the heat meets within them."

Another answer: When the rich man sees the poor man, he withdraws; and when a gathering brings him together with him, he turns away from him and presents him his back. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 36:

(p-432) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah﴾. The commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning the nasi' (intercalation) that the Arabs used to practise, so that their pilgrimage would sometimes fall in Ramadan, sometimes in Shawwal, and so on. They would declare the Muharram lawful in one year and make Safar sacred in its place, and at other times they would make Muharram sacred and declare Safar lawful. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah, mighty and majestic, informed that the number of the months of the Muslims, which they were worshipped by taking as their year, is twelve months according to the phases of the moon. Their pilgrimage and their festivals were fixed according to this number, so at times the Hajj and the fasting fall in winter and at times in summer. This is unlike what the People of the Book rely upon, for they reckon the year as three hundred and sixty-five days and a part of a day. The majority of the reciters read the ʿayn of ﴿ithnā ʿashara﴾ with a fatha. Abu Jaʿfar read ithnā ʿashara, aḥada ʿashara and tisʿata ʿashara with the ʿayn vowelled with a sukun in all of them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾, i.e., in the Preserved Tablet. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the Imam (the Register) which is with Allah, its books. ﴿On the day He created the heavens and the earth, of them four are sacred﴾. Concerning these there are two opinions.

One: they are Rajab, Dhu al-Qaʿda, Dhu al-Hijja and Muharram. This was said by most of the scholars. Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: He named them sacred (ḥurum) for two reasons.

One: the prohibition of fighting in them, and the people of the Jahiliyya too believed in this. The second: that violating the prohibitions in them is a greater sin than violating them in other months, and likewise honouring acts of obedience in them is greater.

(p-433) The second: they are the months in which the polytheists were granted a respite for travel. This was mentioned by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: that is the upright judgement. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that is the correct reckoning and the even count. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾. They differed about the pronoun in ﴿therein﴾ (fihinna) into two opinions.

One: it refers to the twelve months. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. According to this, the meaning is: do not make their sacred things lawful or their lawful things sacred, as the people of the nasi' did.

The second: it refers to the four sacred months. This is the saying of Qatada and al-Farra'. He argued that the Arabs say, for the numbers between three and ten: "thalāth layālin khalawna" (three nights have passed) and "ayyām khalawna" (days have passed); but when they exceed ten they say "khalat wa madat" (it passed); and they say for the numbers between three and ten: "hunna" and "ha'ulā'" (these, feminine plural), but when they exceed ten they say "hiya" and "hadhihi" (this, feminine singular), wishing to show the mark of the few versus the many. Ibn al-Anbari said: the Arabs use the hā' and nūn for a small number, and the hā' and alif for a large number; the paucity is what lies between three and ten, and the abundance is what exceeds ten. They say: "I sent you rams, so slaughter them (fa-dhbahhunna), and rams (kibāsh), so slaughter it (fa-dhbahhā)." Therefore He said: ﴿of them four are sacred﴾ and He said ﴿so do not wrong yourselves therein﴾, because by "therein" (fihinna) He means the four.

As for those among the commentators who said that by His saying "therein" He means the twelve, that is possible, because the Arabs sometimes give the mark of the few to the many and the mark of the many to the few. According to the opinion of the one who said that "therein" returns to the four, there are four opinions regarding the meaning of wronging therein.

(p-434) One: it means sins. The benefit of singling out the prohibition of it in these months is that the matter of sins is magnified in them more than in other times, because of their excellence over others, like His saying: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqara 98], though both are included in the category of angels; and His saying: ﴿fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman 68], though both are included in the category of fruit; and His saying: ﴿so there is to be no obscenity, no transgression and no disputing during the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqara 197], though these are forbidden outside the Hajj too; and as He commanded guarding the middle prayer, though He commanded guarding the others as well. This is the saying of the majority.

The second: that by wronging therein is meant the act of nasi', which is making a sacred month lawful and making a lawful month sacred. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The third: that it is beginning fighting in them, so the meaning is: do not wrong yourselves by fighting in them, unless you are the ones who begin the fighting. This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: that it is abandoning fighting in them, so the meaning is: do not wrong yourselves therein by abandoning the war against your enemy. This was said by Ibn Bahr, and it is the reverse of Muqatil's opinion. The secret in Allah's exalting some months above others is that restraining oneself from desires in them becomes a means to sustaining restraint in other months, a gradual step for the soul toward parting from what it is accustomed to and what is legally disliked.

**The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the an-Nasi' (postponement, the intercalation of months) is only an increase in disbelief﴾.** The majority read *an-Nasi'* with a hamza, with a long vowel after the *nun* and a kasra under the *sin*: **النَّسِيءُ**.

Shibl related from Ibn Kathir that it is read **النَّسْءُ**, on the pattern of **النَّسْعِ**. In another narration from Shibl, it is read **النَّسِيُّ** with a doubled *ya'* and no hamza, which is the reading of Abu Ja'far. The meaning of the word is postponement. The philologists said: *an-Nasi'* is the postponement of a thing.

The Arabs used to forbid the four sacred months, and they held to this as part of the religion of Ibrahim. Sometimes they needed to make lawful what was forbidden because of a war that arose between them. So they would postpone the sanctity of the forbidden month until Safar. Then they would need to postpone Safar as well to the month after it. The months would keep shifting, one month after another, until the prohibition came around to cover the whole year. It was as if they were borrowing the sacred month and lending it out. So God, Mighty and Majestic, informed them that this is an increase in their disbelief, because they made lawful what is unlawful and made unlawful what is lawful, ﴿in order to match the number of what Allah has forbidden﴾, that is, in order to agree with it, so that they would not step outside the prohibition of four months. They would say: "This is equivalent to the four sacred months," and they did not care about making the unlawful lawful and the lawful unlawful.

This practice was done only in Dhu al-Hijjah, when the Arabs gathered for the season (of pilgrimage). Al-Farra' said: In the pre-Islamic period, when they wanted to leave Mina, a man from Banu Kinanah called Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah would stand up. He was the leader of the season, and he would say: "I am the one who is not blamed, not opposed, and whose judgment is not rejected." They would say: "Postpone for us a month," meaning: delay for us the sanctity of the forbidden month and place it in Safar. And he would do so. What led them to this was that three sacred months came in a row, during which they did not raid, and their livelihood came from raiding. So the months would rotate, as we have explained.

It was also said: they would make the forbidden month lawful for a year, and when the following year came, they would return it to its prohibition. Abu 'Ubayd said: The first explanation is more beloved to me, because this view does not involve the rotation of the months.

Mujahid said: The first person to introduce the an-Nasi' was Janadah ibn 'Awf al-Kinani. The pilgrimage of Abu Bakr coincided with Dhu al-Qa'dah. Then the Prophet ﷺ performed the pilgrimage in the following year in Dhu al-Hijjah. That is when he said: "Indeed, time has returned to the form it had on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." Al-Kalbi said: The first person to do this was Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah.

**The words of the Exalted: ﴿by which those who disbelieved are led astray﴾.** Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read **يَضِلُّ** with a fatha on the *ya'* and a kasra on the *dad*, meaning that they earn misguidance through it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read **يَضَلُّ**... more precisely **يُضَلُّ** with a damma on the *ya'* and a fatha on the *dad*, in the passive form, with no named agent. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Ya'qub, except al-Walid, read **يُضِلُّ** with a damma on the *ya'* and a kasra on the *dad*. This reading has three possible meanings:

First: Allah misguides by it. Second: Satan misguides by it. Both of these were mentioned by Ibn al-Qasim. Third: those who disbelieved lead people astray by it, because they are the ones who instituted it for them.

Abu 'Ali said: The implied meaning is: those who disbelieved lead their followers astray by it.

Ibn al-Qasim said: The pronoun in **بِهِ** ("by it") refers to an-Nasi'. The root of an-Nasi' is *al-mansu'*, meaning "the postponed," and it shifts from the pattern *maf'ul* to *fa'il*, as in **مَطْبُوخٌ** and **طَبِيخٌ**, and **مَقْدُورٌ** and **قَدِيرٌ**. He also said: It was said that the pronoun refers to *adh-dhulm* (wrongdoing), because an-Nasi' revealed the interpretation of the wrongdoing, so it takes the place of something made manifest. The first view is our preferred one.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 38:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What is wrong with you, that when you are told, "Go forth (infiru) in the way of Allah"﴾. The exegetes said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the expedition to Tabuk, and it was a time of hardship, drought, and intense heat, and the fruits had ripened, this weighed heavily upon the people and they loved to remain behind, so this verse was revealed."

His saying, "What is wrong with you" (ma lakum), is an interrogative whose meaning is reproach. His saying, "Go forth" (infiru), means: set out. The root of nafar (going forth) is leaving one place for another because of a matter that stirs one to do so. His saying, ﴿you cling heavily to the earth (ithaqaltum)﴾: Ibn Qutaybah said: he intended tathaqaltum, so the taa was assimilated into the thaa, and an alif was introduced so that what follows it would be vowelled with sukun; and he intended: "you sat down." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash it is "tathaqaltum."

Regarding the meaning of "to the earth" (ila al-ard) there are three opinions.

The first: you clung to the desires of the world when the earth brought forth its fruit; this is related from Mujahid.

The second: you were content with (itma'nantum ila) the world; this is related from al-Dahhak.

The third: you clung to remaining in your land; this is related from al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ That is, with its pleasures in comparison with the pleasures of the Hereafter; for what is enjoyed in this world is little compared with what the friends of Allah enjoy in Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 39:

[p. 438] His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Unless you go forth, He will punish you﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged them to campaign against the Romans, they were reluctant. So this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Others said: this applies specifically to those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called to go forth but who did not go. Ibn Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called a tribe of the Arabs to go forth, but they were reluctant to go with him, so He withheld rain from them, and that was their punishment."

In His statement ﴿and replace you with a people other than you﴾ there is a severe warning against staying behind from jihad, and an announcement that He will replace them with people who are not reluctant, to support His Prophet. Then He informed them that if they abandon supporting him, they will not harm him, just as it did not harm him when he was in Makkah. Regarding the pronoun in "you will not harm him" there are two views.

The first: it refers to Allah, and the meaning is: do not harm Allah by abandoning going forth. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the meaning is: do not harm him by abandoning his support. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Section

It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Ikrimah that they said: His statement ﴿Unless you go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ was abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by His statement ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: this is not among the abrogated verses, since there is no contradiction between the two verses, and the ruling of each verse remains in force in its own context. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la reported from some scholars that they said: there is no abrogation here. Whenever the people of the frontier towns (thughur) cannot withstand the enemy, it becomes an obligation on the people to go forth to them, and whenever they are able to manage without the help of those behind them, those who remain behind are excused. Others said that this applies to the expedition of Tabuk, when going forth with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became obligatory upon the people.

(p-439) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Unless you support him﴾, meaning: by going forth with him, ﴿then God has already supported him﴾, a help against his enemies; ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾, when they intended to destroy him, as we explained in His saying: ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal 8:30]. So He informed them that His support for him does not depend on them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿the second of two﴾. The Arabs say: "He is the second of two" (thani ithnayn), meaning one of the two, and "the third of three" (thalith thalatha), meaning one of the three. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿the second of two﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The meaning: God has supported him as one of two, that is, He supported him while alone except for Abu Bakr.

This is also the meaning of the saying of al-Sha'bi: "God rebuked all the people of the earth in this verse except Abu Bakr."

Ibn Jarir said: The meaning is: they expelled him while he was one of two, and they were the Messenger of God ﷺ and Abu Bakr. As for the cave (al-ghar), it is a hole in a mountain. Ibn Faris said: al-ghar is a cave; al-ghar is a fragrant plant; al-ghar is a group of people; and al-gharan are the belly and the private part, and they are the two hollow places. It is said: "He is only a slave of his two hollows." The poet said:

Did you not see that time is a day and a night, and that the young man strives constantly for his two hollows?

Qatada said: This cave is in a mountain in Makkah called Thawr. Mujahid said: The two of them remained in it for three days. I have mentioned the hadith of the Hijrah in my book "al-Hada'iq".

Anas ibn Malik said: (p-440) God, Mighty and Majestic, commanded a tree, and it grew in front of the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ and shielded him. He commanded the spider, and it wove across his face. He commanded two wild doves, and they landed at the mouth of the cave. When they (the pursuers) approached the cave, one of them hurried to look, saw the two doves, and returned saying: "I saw two doves at the mouth of the cave, so I knew that no one was in it."

Muqatil said: A tracker (al-qa'if) came, looked at the footprints, and said: "This is the footprint of Ibn Abi Quhafa, and the other I do not recognize, except that it resembles the footprint that is in the Maqam." The companion in this verse is Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr had wept when the polytheists passed by the entrance of the cave, so the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "What do you think of two whose third is God?"

Regarding al-sakina (tranquility) there are three opinions.

One: it is mercy; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is dignity (al-waqar); this was said by Qatada. The third: it is calm and tranquility (al-sukun wal-tuma'ninah); this was said by Ibn Qutayba, and it is the most sound.

Regarding the pronoun in "ʿalayhi" (upon him) there are three opinions.

One: it refers back to Abu Bakr; this is the view of Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, and Habib ibn Abi Thabit. Those who supported this view argued that the Prophet ﷺ was already tranquil.

The second: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ; this was said by Muqatil. (p-441) The third: the pronoun here carries the sense of the dual, and the implied meaning is: "God sent down His tranquility upon both of them," but the mention was reduced to one of them rather than repeated for both, like His saying: ﴿And God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawba 9:62]. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And strengthened him﴾, meaning: He strengthened him, referring to the Prophet ﷺ without dispute. ﴿With soldiers you did not see﴾, and they are the angels. When did this happen? There are two views.

One: on the day of Badr, the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), and the day of Hunayn; this was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: when he was in the cave, the angels turned the faces and sights of the disbelievers away from seeing him; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

If it is said: since there is agreement that the pronoun of object in "ayyadahu" refers to the Prophet ﷺ, how does the pronoun in "ʿalayhi" differ from it, when both are in the same structure of the speech?

The answer: every pronoun is returned to what is most fitting for it. Tranquility is only needed by one who is distressed, and the Prophet ﷺ was not distressed. As for support with angels, it was only for the Prophet ﷺ. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿That you may believe in God and His Messenger, support him, honor him, and glorify Him﴾ [al-Fath 48:8], where "him" refers to the Prophet ﷺ and "glorify Him" refers to God, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾. There are two views concerning it.

One: the word of the disbelievers is polytheism, which God made the lowest because it is subdued, while the word of God, which is monotheism, is the highest because it has prevailed. This is the view of most scholars.

The second: the word of the disbelievers is what they plotted among themselves in their scheming against him to kill him, and the word of God is that He is his helper; this was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrima, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Ya'qub read "wa-kalimata Allah" with the accusative.

(p-442) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And God is Mighty﴾, meaning: in His retribution against the disbelievers, ﴿Wise﴾ in His governance.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 41:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾. The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that al-Miqdad came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was large and heavy-set, so he complained to him and asked him for permission to stay behind, and this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Suddi. Regarding the meaning of "light and heavy," there are eleven opinions.

The first: old and young. This was narrated by Anas from Abu Talhah, and al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Abu Salih, Shammar ibn Atiyyah, and Ibn Zayd, among others, said the same.

The second: on foot and mounted. This was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas, and al-Awza'i said the same.

The third: eager and not eager. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah and Muqatil said the same.

The fourth: rich and poor. This was reported from Ibn Abbas. Then, regarding the meaning of this view, there are two statements. One is that the "light" are those in hardship with few dependants, and the "heavy" are those with dependants and means. This was said by al-Farra'. The second is that the "light" are those of means, and the "heavy" are those in hardship. This was reported from al-Zajjaj.

The fifth: those with dependants and those without. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The sixth: those with property to look after and those without. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The seventh: those with occupations and those without. This was said by al-Hakam.

The eighth: the healthy and the sick. This was said by Murrah al-Hamdani and Juwaybir.

The ninth: the unmarried and the married. This was said by Yaman ibn Rayyab.

The tenth: light toward obedience and heavy against disobedience. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The eleventh: light of weapons and heavy with the accumulation of them. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

**Section**

Ata' al-Khurasani narrated from Ibn Abbas that this verse was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. Al-Suddi said it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves﴾. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: He made jihad with wealth and with the self obligatory together. Whoever has wealth but is ill, or crippled, or too weak to fight, is obligated to perform jihad with his wealth, by giving it to someone else who will go out to fight with it, just as he is obligated to perform jihad with his person if he is strong. If he has wealth and strength, he is obligated to perform jihad with both self and wealth. Whoever is destitute and incapable, his jihad is through sincere counsel to Allah and His Messenger, based on His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

(p-٤٤٤) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is better for you﴾. Regarding this there are two statements.

The first: that is better for you than abandoning it and being sluggish about it.

The second: that jihad is the better outcome for you, ﴿if you knew﴾ what reward you will have.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 42:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had it been a near gain﴾. The exegetes said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. The meaning of the verse: Had what they were called to been a near gain. The ʿaraḍ (worldly goods, gain) is everything of the benefits of this world that presents itself to you. So the meaning: had it been spoils, near at hand, or a journey of ease (qāṣidan), that is, easy and near, they would have followed you, seeking wealth. ﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: al-shuqqa is the journey. al-Zajjaj said: al-shuqqa is the goal that is aimed at. Ibn Fāris said: al-shuqqa is arriving at a distant land; you say: a shuqqa shāqqa (a hard, distant journey).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will swear by Allah﴾, meaning the hypocrites, when you return to them: (Had we been able) and Zāʾida related from al-Aʿmash, and al-Aṣmaʿī from Nāfiʿ, the reading "lawu istaṭaʿnā" with a ḍamma on the waw, and likewise wherever it occurs, like ﴿lawi ṭṭalaʿta ʿalayhim﴾ [al-Kahf 18]. It seems that when the waw needed a vowel, it was vowelled with a ḍamma because it is the sister of the waw (the vowel of the same kind). The meaning: had we been capable and had we had ample wealth. (They would destroy themselves) by lying and hypocrisy. ﴿And Allah knows that they are indeed liars﴾, because they were wealthy and did not go out.

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾

The Prophet (ﷺ) had granted permission to some of the hypocrites (al-munafiqin) to stay behind when he set out for Tabuk. Ibn Abbas said: "On that day he did not yet know who the hypocrites were." Amr ibn Maymun said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did two things for which he had not been commanded: his granting permission to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom (al-fida') from the captives. So Allah rebuked him, as you hear." Muwriq said: "His Lord rebuked him for this." Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: "Look at this gentleness. He began with the pardon before reproaching him for the sin." Ibn al-Anbari said: "He was not addressed this way for a crime he had committed. Rather, Allah honoured him and raised his standing when He opened the speech with the words ﴿May Allah pardon you﴾, just as a man says to someone who is dear to him: 'May Allah pardon you, what did you do about my need?' and 'May Allah be pleased with you, why did you not visit me?'"

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿until those who were truthful become clear to you﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: its meaning is, "until you know those with a valid excuse for staying behind from those who have no excuse."

The second: "Had you not given them permission, they would have stayed behind, and their lying in their excuses would have become clear to you." Qatada said: "Then Allah the Exalted abrogated (naskh, the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation) this verse with His words: ﴿so give permission to whom you will among them﴾ [al-Nur: 62]."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verses 44–45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who believe in Allah do not ask you for permission﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: This is a rebuke to the hypocrites when they asked for permission to remain behind. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informed His Prophet ﷺ that the sign of hypocrisy at that time was asking for permission.

(p-446) * Section

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: This verse was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿They do not depart until they seek his permission…﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nur: 62]. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: There is no room for abrogation here, since both verses can be acted upon. That is because He only censured the hypocrites for asking his permission to stay behind from jihad without an excuse, while He permitted the believers to ask permission for a need that arises for them. When the hypocrites were with him and a need arose for them, they would leave without asking his permission.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 46–47:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they had wanted to go forth﴾ meaning: those who asked permission from him to remain behind.

Concerning the meaning of "equipment" (al-'uddah) there are two opinions.

The first: it is the intention (al-niyyah). This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is weapons, mounts, and whatever is suitable for going forth. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. "Al-inbi'ath" (being roused) means setting off. "Al-tathbit" (holding back) means your turning a person away from something he is doing.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it was said, "Remain [behind] with those who remain."﴾ Concerning who said this to them, there are three opinions.

The first: they were inspired with this as a forsaking (khudhlan) of them. This was said by Muqatil. The second: the Prophet ﷺ said it in anger at them. The third: it was the statement of some of them to others. Al-Mawardi mentioned these two.

(p-447) Concerning the meaning of "those who remain" there are two opinions.

The first: they are those who remain without an excuse. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: they are those who remain with an excuse, such as women and children. This was mentioned by 'Ali ibn 'Isa.

Al-Zajjaj said: Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed of why He disliked their going forth, saying: ﴿Had they gone forth among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption﴾. And "khabal" means corruption and the loss of a thing. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Khabal" means evil.

If it is said: Was there corruption among the Companions, such that it was said, "they would not have increased you except in corruption"? The answer: this is an exceptive of disconnected type (al-istithna' al-munqati'), and the meaning is: they would not have increased you in strength, but rather they would have caused corruption among you. It was also said: the occasion of revelation of this verse was that when the Prophet ﷺ set out, he pitched his army at Thaniyyat al-Wada', and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy went forth and pitched his army lower than that; when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ marched on, Ibn Ubayy remained behind along with those hypocrites who remained behind, and this verse was revealed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they would have hastened between you [spreading discord]﴾. Al-Farra' said: "al-iyda'" is traveling quickly among the people. Abu 'Ubaydah said: they would have hastened among you, and its root is from "al-takhallul" (penetrating through). Al-Zajjaj said: it is said, "awda'tu fi al-sayr", meaning I hastened in the journey.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿seeking to cause you discord﴾. Al-Farra' said: they seek it for you. Concerning "fitnah" there are two opinions.

The first: disbelief. This was said by al-Dahhak, Muqatil, and Ibn Qutaybah.

(p-448) The second: the splitting of the community and the scattering of the word. al-Hasan said: they would have hastened between you with tale-bearing, to corrupt your relations.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: spies who convey your news to them. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The second: those who hear their speech and obey them. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 48:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they had sought discord﴾. Regarding "discord" (al-fitnah) there are two opinions.

The first: evil. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: polytheism (shirk). This is related from Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from before﴾, meaning: from before the expedition of Tabuk.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and they turned over matters for you﴾, there are five opinions.

The first: they plotted against you with treacherous schemes. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has also been said that twelve men of the hypocrites stood on his path at night in order to assassinate him, but Allah protected him from them.

The second: they devised ways to scatter your affair and to nullify your religion. This is related from Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn Jarir said: this is like the withdrawal of Ibn Ubayy with his companions on the day of Uhud.

The third: that it is their saying what is not in their hearts.

The fourth: that it is their inclination toward you outwardly, and their backing of the polytheists inwardly.

The fifth: that they swore to them by Allah, "If we had been able, we would have gone out with you." Al-Mawardi mentioned these three opinions.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until the truth came﴾, meaning: the victory; and ﴿the command of Allah became manifest﴾, meaning: Islam.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 49:

(p-449) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is one who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial."﴾ The occasion of its revelation: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to al-Jadd ibn Qays, 'O Jadd, would you like to take part in the battle against the sons of al-Asfar (the Byzantines)? Perhaps you might seize some of the daughters of al-Asfar.' He said, 'O Messenger of Allah, grant me permission to stay behind, and do not put me to trial with the daughters of al-Asfar.' So he turned away from him and said, 'I have granted you permission,' and this verse was revealed." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. This verse and what follows it, up to His saying, ﴿Indeed, the charities are only...﴾ (9:60), concern the hypocrites.

His saying, exalted is He: "And among them" meaning the hypocrites, "is one who says, 'Grant me permission'" i.e., to remain behind from jihad, and he is al-Jadd ibn Qays. Regarding His saying, ﴿and do not put me to trial﴾, there are four opinions.

The first: "Do not put me to trial with women." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: "Do not make me commit sin by your ordering me to go out, which is not easy for me, so I would sin by disobeying you." This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Zajjaj.

The third: "Do not make me a disbeliever by your compelling me to go out." This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: "Do not divert me from my affairs." This was said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely, into temptation they have fallen﴾. Regarding this temptation, there are four opinions.

The first: that it is disbelief. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The second: distress (haraj), said by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. The third: sin, said by Qatadah and al-Zajjaj. The fourth: the punishment of Hell, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verses 50–51:

(p-450) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If good befalls you﴾, that is: victory and spoils of war. And "affliction" (al-musibah) is: killing and defeat. (They say: "We had already taken our precaution") that is: we acted with caution and did not go out. (And they turn away, rejoicing) at your affliction and their own safety.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except what Allah has decreed for us﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first: what He has decreed against us. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: what He has made clear to us in His Books, that we will either be victorious, and that will be a good outcome for us, or we will be killed, and martyrdom will be a good outcome for us too. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: "Nothing will befall us in the end of our affair except what Allah has decreed for us of the victory He promised us." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He is our Protector﴾, that is: our Helper.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 52:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Do you await for us anything except one of the two best outcomes (al-husnayayn)?"﴾ That is, "Do you wait (tarabbusun)?" The two best outcomes are: victory and martyrdom. ﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself﴾ There are two opinions concerning this punishment.

(p-451) One of them: thunderbolts (al-sawa'iq), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: death, said by Ibn Jurayj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or by our hands﴾ meaning: killing.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Spend, willingly or unwillingly﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "Al-Jadd ibn Qays said to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he proposed to him the expedition against the Romans: 'When I see the women, I become tempted; but this is my wealth, I will help you with it.' So this verse was revealed," said Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Zajjaj said: This is in the form of a command, but its meaning is that of a conditional and its consequence: the meaning is, "If you spend willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted from you." A parallel to this in poetry is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"Treat us badly or treat us well, you will not be blamed by us, nor will you be rejected, if you turn away."

He did not command her to do wrong, but informed her that whether she did wrong or good, he would remain faithful to her covenant. Al-Farra' said: A similar example is ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:80].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And nothing prevents their expenditures from being accepted from them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "tuqbala" with a ta'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yuqbala" with a ya'. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with the ta', it is because the verb is attributed to a feminine noun in form; and whoever reads with the ya', it is because it is not a true feminization, so it is permissible to make it masculine, as in His saying: ﴿Then whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. Al-Jahdari read "an yaqbala" with an open ya', and "nafaqatihim" with a kasra on the ta'. Al-A'mash read "nafaqatuhum" without an alif, with the ta' in the nominative. Abu Mijlaz and Abu Raja' read "an yaqbala" with a ya', and "nafaqatahum" with a fatha on the ta', in the singular.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except that they disbelieved in Allah﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: the "anna" here is with a fatha, because it is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), being in the nominative after "mana'ahum" (prevented them). The meaning is: nothing prevented the acceptance of their expenditure from them except their disbelief in Allah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except while they are lazy﴾. We have explained it in Surat an-Nisa' (4:142).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they do not spend except while they are unwilling﴾. Because they regard spending as a burden (maghram).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let not their wealth impress you﴾, i.e., do not admire what We have bestowed upon them of wealth and children. There are four opinions regarding the meaning of the verse.

The first: ﴿So let not their wealth impress you, nor their children; indeed, Allah intends only to punish them with them in this worldly life﴾. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah. According to this view, there is an inversion of order in the verse, and their punishment in the Hereafter is for what they did in acquiring wealth and spending it.

The second: that the verse is according to its own arrangement, and the meaning is: Allah intends to punish them with them in this world through calamities affecting their wealth and children, so these are a punishment for them, while for the believers they are a reward. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that the meaning is: Allah intends to punish them by taking zakat from their wealth and by spending in the way of Allah. This was said by al-Hasan. According to this view, the pronoun refers to wealth alone.

The fourth: Allah intends to punish them by taking their children captive and seizing their wealth as spoils. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. According to this view, the verse refers to the polytheists.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their souls depart﴾, i.e., they go out. It is said: "zahaqa al-sahm" means the arrow passed beyond its target.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verses 56–57:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you﴾, meaning: they are believers. And (yufarriqun) means "they fear."

As for al-malja', al-Zajjaj said: al-malja' and al-laja' (both) are maqsur and mahmuz, and it is the place in which one takes refuge and fortifies oneself. Al-magharat is the plural of maghara, which is the place into which a person goes deep (yaghur), that is, in which he hides himself.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "aw maghurat" with a damma on the mim, because it is said: aghertu and ghirtu, when you enter the ghawr (the depression or cave).

The original form of mudkhal is mudtakhil, but the ta' is changed to dal after the dal, because the ta' is mahmusa (voiceless) and the dal is majhura (voiced), and the ta' and the dal come from the same point of articulation, so the speech becomes lighter by one aspect.

Ubayy, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu al-Jawza' read "aw mutadakhkhilan" with a raised mim, with a fathah on the ta' and the dal, and the kha' doubled (shaddah). Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran read "mundakhalan" with a nun after the damma-ed mim. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ya'qub read "mudkhalan" with a fathah on the mim, and the dal lightened and sukun.

Al-Zajjaj said: whoever says "madkhalan" (with fathah on mim) it is from dakhala yadkhulu madkhalan; and whoever says "mudkhalan" (with damma on mim) it is from adkhaltuhu madkhalan. The poet said:

Praise be to Allah, as we pass the evening and as we greet the morning with good, my Lord has greeted us and has evened us out.

The meaning of mudda'khal is: if they found a people into whose group they could enter, they would turn to it, that is, to one of these things, ﴿while they rush headlong﴾, meaning: they hasten with a rush that nothing turns their faces back from. It is said: jamaha and tamaha, when he hastened and nothing turned his face back; and from this it is said: a jamuh horse, for the one which, when it charges, the bridle does not turn back.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 58:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾. There are two opinions regarding who this verse was revealed about.

The first: "It was Dhu al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ) one day: 'Be just, O Messenger of Allah!' So this verse was revealed." It is also said he was Abu al-Khawasir, and it is also said he was Ibn Dhi al-Khuwaysira.

The second: It was Tha'laba ibn Hatib, who used to say: "Muhammad only gives to whomever he wishes," so this verse was revealed. Ibn Qutayba said: "Yalmizuka" means he criticizes you and attacks you. It is said: "I hamaztu fulanan wa lamaztuhu," meaning when I backbite him and find fault with him. Most readers recite the mim of "yalmizuka" with a kasra. Ya'qub, Nazif on the authority of Qunbul, Aban on the authority of Asim, and al-Qazzaz on the authority of Abd al-Warith recited "yalmizun" (in the verse of al-Tawba: 79) and "yalmizuka," and "talmizu" (in al-Hujurat: 11), with a damma on the mim in all of them. Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "yulamizuka," in the pattern of "yufa'iluka." Hammad ibn Salama narrated it from Ibn Kathir. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "It is necessary that this form, tafa'alta, be from someone, like: 'tarraqtu al-na'l' (I mended the sandal) and 'a'afahu Allah' (may Allah grant him well-being), because this cannot come from the Prophet (ﷺ)." Al-A'mash recited "yalmizuka" with a shadda on the mim without an alif, in the pattern of "yufi'iluka."

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "lamaztu al-rajula almizuhu wa almuzuhu," with a kasra and a damma on the mim, when you criticize him. Likewise: "hamaztuhu ahmizuhu." The poet said:

When I meet you, you show me flattery,
but when you are absent, you become the slanderer and the defamer.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 9, verses 59–60:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them﴾, meaning they were content with what they were given. ﴿And said, "Indeed, to Allah we are eager [for more]"﴾, meaning eager for increase. That is, it would have been better for them. This is the answer to "law" (*law*, "if only"), and it is omitted in the wording.

Then He explained who deserves the alms (*al-sadaqat*, obligatory charity) by His words: ﴿Alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾. The scholars differed about the description of the *faqir* (poor) and the *miskin* (needy) in six opinions.

The first: the *faqir* is the one who abstains from asking, and the *miskin* is the one who asks while still having some breath left in him. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Zuhri, al-Hakam, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

The second: the *faqir* is the needy person who is afflicted with a disability (*zamanah*), and the *miskin* is the needy person who has no disability. This was said by Qatadah.

(p-456) The third: the *faqir* is the emigrant (*muhajir*), and the *miskin* is the one who did not emigrate. This was said by al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim and al-Nakha'i.

The fourth: the *faqir* is the poor among the Muslims, and the *miskin* is from among the People of the Book. This was said by Ikrimah.

The fifth: the *faqir* is the one who has a means of subsistence (*al-balghah*) of something, and the *miskin* is the one who has nothing at all. This was said by Abu Hanifah, Yunus ibn Habib, Ya'qub ibn al-Sikkit and Ibn Qutaybah. They argued from the words of the poet al-Ra'i:

*As for the poor man (faqir), whose milch-camel suffices for his dependants, and whom no sheep-or-camel leaves without something...*

He called him a *faqir*, while he had a milch-camel that sufficed him and his dependants. Yunus said: I said to a Bedouin, "Are you a *faqir*?" He said: "No, by Allah, rather I am a *miskin*," meaning that he was in a worse condition than the *faqir*.

The sixth: the *faqir* is in greater need than the *miskin*. This is the view of Ahmad, because the *faqir* is derived from the breaking of the spine (*inkisar al-fiqar*), while *maskanah* is derived from stillness and humility (*al-sukun wal-khushu'*), and that is more emphatic. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is narrated from al-Asma'i that he said: the *miskin* is in a better condition than the *faqir*. Ahmad ibn Ubayd said: the *miskin* is in a better condition than the *faqir*, because the origin of *faqir* in the language is *mafqur*, the one whose spine has been removed from his back's vertebrae (*fiqar*), so it is as if his back was broken from the severity of poverty; then it was changed from *mafqur* to *faqir*, as it is said *majruh* and *jarih*, *matbukh* and *tabikh*. The poet said:

*When he saw the vultures' feathers scattering, he raised his forelegs like the unarmed poor man (faqir)...*

He said: Among the evidence for this view is His saying: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy men (*masakin*) who worked on the sea﴾ (al-Kahf 18:79). So the description of *maskanah* was applied to one who owned a boat worth wealth. He said: This is the correct view according to us.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾. These are the collectors (*al-su'at*) who gather the alms, and they are given from it according to the wages of their like, and what they take is not zakat.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾. These are people whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would win over to Islam by giving them, and they were people of standing. They are of two kinds: Muslims and disbelievers. As for the Muslims, they are of two kinds: one whose intentions in Islam were weak, so he was won over to strengthen his intention, like Uyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Aqra'; and one whose intentions were good, but he was given to win over his tribe from the polytheists, like Adi ibn Hatim. As for the polytheists, they are of two kinds: one who targets the Muslims with harm, so he was won over to repel his harm, like Amir ibn al-Tufayl; and one who had an inclination towards Islam, so he was won over with a gift so that he would believe, like Safwan ibn Umayyah. I have mentioned the number of those whose hearts are to be reconciled in my book *al-Talqih*. Their ruling remains according to Ahmad in one narration, while Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said their ruling has been abrogated (*mansukh*). Al-Zuhri said: I do not know of anything that abrogated the ruling of those whose hearts are to be reconciled.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and for captives (*fi al-riqab*)﴾. We have mentioned it in Surah al-Baqarah (2:177).

(p-458) His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and the debtors﴾. These are those upon whom debt has become binding and who cannot find the means to repay it. Qatadah said: They are people who owe debts without having been corrupt, extravagant or wasteful. He only said this because it cannot be assured, regarding one who is corrupt, that if his debt is paid he will not return to borrowing for the same purpose. There is no disagreement about the permissibility of paying his debt and giving him zakat, but Qatadah said it out of disapproval.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and in the way of Allah﴾, meaning: the raiders (*ghuzat*) and those stationed on the frontier (*al-murabitin*). According to us it is permissible to give to those among them who are wealthy as well as to those who are poor; this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: only the poor among them are given. Is it permissible to spend from zakat on the pilgrimage (*hajj*) or not? On this there are two narrations from Ahmad.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabil*)﴾. He is the traveller who has been cut off from his means, even if he has wealth in his own land; this was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, Abu Hanifah and Ahmad. As for one who intends to begin a journey, is it permissible to give him? Al-Shafi'i said: it is permissible, and a similar view is reported from Ahmad. We have mentioned the views of the exegetes on this in Surah al-Baqarah (2:177).

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿as an obligation from Allah﴾, meaning that Allah has made this obligatory.

**Section**

According to our companions, the limit of the wealthy person who is prevented from taking zakat is one of two things: that he owns fifty dirhams or its equivalent in gold, whether or not that suffices for his maintenance. The second: that he has sufficient means, either from a trade, or from the rent of property, or from merchandise (*'urud*) for trade (p-459), whose profit suffices for his maintenance. Abu Hanifah said: the criterion in this is that he owns a *nisab* (minimum threshold) on which zakat is obligatory. As for those close relatives (*dhawu al-qurba*) for whom the sadaqah is forbidden, they are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. Abu Hanifah said: it is forbidden for the descendants of Hashim, but not for the descendants of al-Muttalib. It is permissible for someone from the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib to work in collecting the sadaqah and take his wages from it, contrary to Abu Hanifah. As for the clients (*mawali*) of the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, the sadaqah is forbidden for them, contrary to Malik. It is not permissible to give one's sadaqah to someone whose maintenance one is obligated to provide; this was said by Malik and al-Thawri. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: one does not give to one's parent, however high, nor to one's child, however low, nor to one's spouse, but one gives to anyone other than them. As for the *dhimmi* (non-Muslim protected subject), most scholars hold that it is not permissible to give to him. Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: if one does not find a Muslim, the *dhimmi* may be given. It is not obligatory to cover all the categories, nor to consider a specific number from each category; this is the view of Abu Hanifah and Malik. Al-Shafi'i said: it is obligatory to cover each category with at least three persons.

As for when one wishes to transfer the sadaqah from the land of the wealth to a place where the prayer is shortened, it is not permissible for him to do so; if he transfers it, it does not suffice for him. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: transferring it is disliked, but it suffices. Ahmad said: one does not give the poor person more than fifty dirhams. Abu Hanifah said: I dislike that a single person be given two hundred dirhams from zakat, but if you give it, it suffices for you. As for al-Shafi'i, he considered what removes the need without a fixed limit. If one gives to someone he thinks is poor, and it becomes clear that he is wealthy, is it sufficient? On this there are two narrations from Ahmad.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 9, verses 59–60:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them﴾, meaning they were content with what they were given. ﴿And said, "Indeed, to Allah we are eager [for more]"﴾, meaning eager for increase. That is, it would have been better for them. This is the answer to "law" (*law*, "if only"), and it is omitted in the wording.

Then He explained who deserves the alms (*al-sadaqat*, obligatory charity) by His words: ﴿Alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾. The scholars differed about the description of the *faqir* (poor) and the *miskin* (needy) in six opinions.

The first: the *faqir* is the one who abstains from asking, and the *miskin* is the one who asks while still having some breath left in him. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Zuhri, al-Hakam, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

The second: the *faqir* is the needy person who is afflicted with a disability (*zamanah*), and the *miskin* is the needy person who has no disability. This was said by Qatadah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 61:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions. (p-460) The first: "Khidham ibn Khalid, al-Jullas ibn Suwayd, Ubayd ibn Hilal, and others, used to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Some of them said to others: 'Do not do this, for we fear that he will be informed and it will fall upon us.' Al-Jullas said: 'Rather, we will say whatever we wish, for Muhammad is only a listening ear. Then we will come to him and he will believe us.' So this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "A man among the hypocrites called Nabtal ibn al-Harith used to carry the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the hypocrites. It was said to him: 'Do not do this.' He said: 'Muhammad is only an ear; whoever tells him something, he believes him. We say whatever we wish, then we come to him and swear to him, and he believes us.' So this verse was revealed." This was stated by Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

The third: "Some hypocrites, among them al-Jullas ibn Suwayd and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, gathered and wished to attack the Prophet (ﷺ). With them was a young man from the Ansar called Amir ibn Qays, and they belittled him. They spoke and said: 'If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys.' The young man became angry and said: 'By Allah, what Muhammad says is true, and you are worse than donkeys.' Then he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. He summoned them and questioned them, and they swore that Amir was lying. Amir swore that they had lied and said: 'O Allah, do not separate us until You show the truthfulness of the truthful and the lying of the liar.' So this verse was revealed," and the words ﴿They swear to Allah before you to please you﴾ were revealed. This was stated by al-Suddi. As for the harm, it is his disparagement and the transmission of his words. The meaning of (udhun) is one who accepts everything that is said to him. (p-461)

Ibn Qutaybah said: The root of this is that the ear is that which hears, so whoever believes every report he hears is called "udhun." The majority of reciters read (هُوَ أُذُنٌ قُلْ أُذُنُ) with the doubled dhal. Nafi' read "هُوَ أُذْنٌ قُلْ أذْنٌ خَيْرٌ" with the dhal sukun in both. The meaning of "أُذُنُ خَيْرٍ لَكُمْ" is: an ear of good for you, not an ear of evil; it hears good and acts upon it, and does not act upon evil when it hears it. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ibn Abi Abla read "أُذُنٌ" with tanwin and "خَيْرٌ" with raf'. The meaning: if it is as you say, he hears from you and believes you, which is better for you than that he should call you liars. Abu Ali said: It is permissible to apply "ear" to the whole person, as al-Khalil said: the camel's "nab" was so named because of the place of the mature tooth, so the whole was named after it; they applied the name of the organ to the whole because of the frequency of its use for listening.

Then he clarified who accepts, saying ﴿He believes in Allah and believes the believers﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: the ba' and lam are extra; the meaning is: he confirms Allah and confirms the believers. Al-Zajjaj said: he hears what Allah sends down to him, so he believes in it, and believes the believers in what they inform him. ﴿And a mercy﴾, i.e., he is a mercy, because he was the cause of the faith of the believers. Hamzah read "wa-rahmatin" with the genitive. Abu Ali said: the meaning is: an ear of good and mercy, meaning: one who listens to good and mercy.

Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 9, verse 62:

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. On this there are two opinions.

The first: by repentance (*tawbah*) and turning back (*inabah*). The second: by abandoning criticism and blame.

If it is asked: Why did He say "*yurḍūhu*" (they should please Him, singular pronoun) and not "*yurḍawhumā*" (they should please them both)? We have explained this at His words, ﴿and they do not spend it in the cause of Allah﴾ [At-Tawbah: 34].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 63:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not know﴾. Abu Zayd narrated from al-Mufaddal: "Do you not know" with the ta' (second person).

﴿That whoever opposes Allah﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

The first: whoever opposes Allah. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said.

The second: whoever is hostile to Allah, like your saying: "whoever stands aloof from Allah and His Messenger," meaning: he is in one limit (ḥadd), while Allah and His Messenger are in another limit.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then indeed for him is the fire of Hell﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "fa-anna" with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Abu Razin, Abu 'Imran, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with a kasrah. Whoever reads with a kasrah, it is on the basis of a fresh sentence (isti'naf) after the fa', as you say: "fa-lahu nar Jahannam" (so for him is the fire of Hell). The particle "inna" (indeed) has entered as an emphasizer. As for whoever says "fa-anna lahu" (with fatḥah), he repeated the first "anna" for emphasis, because when the statement was lengthened, repeating it was more emphatic. (p-463)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 64:

Allah's words: ﴿The hypocrites fear lest a surah be sent down about them﴾ (yahdharu al-munafiqun). Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three reports.

The first: "The hypocrites used to disparage the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among themselves, saying, 'Perhaps Allah will not expose our secret.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid.

The second: Some of the hypocrites said, "I wish I had been flogged a hundred lashes, and that nothing would be revealed about us that would expose us." So this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: A group of the hypocrites lay in wait for the Prophet (ﷺ) on a dark night on his return from Tabuk, intending to assassinate him. Jibril (peace be upon him) informed him, and this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Kaysan.

Regarding His words ﴿The hypocrites fear﴾ there are two views.

The first: It is a report from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, about their state. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah, and it was chosen by Ibn al-Qasim.

The second: It is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to them to be cautious, so its meaning is: "Let the hypocrites beware." This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: The Arabs often present a command in the form of a statement. They say, "May Allah have mercy on the believer, and punish the disbeliever," meaning, "Let Him have mercy and let Him punish." They drop the lam and treat it as a statement in its nominative form, though they intend only supplication, and supplication is in the imperfect form of the command.

Allah's words: ﴿Say: "Mock [as you will]"﴾ (qul istahzi'u). This is a threat, issued in the form of a command, for the purpose of intimidation.

Regarding His words ﴿Indeed, Allah will bring out what you fear﴾ there are two views.

The first: He will make manifest what you conceal. The second: He will support against those whom you forsake. Both were mentioned by al-Mawardi.

[p. 465] His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you ask them﴾ There are six opinions regarding the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "Jadd ibn Qays, Wadi'ah ibn Khudham, and al-Jahir ibn Khamir were walking ahead of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on his return from Tabuk. Two of them began to mock the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while the third laughed at what the two were saying and did not speak anything. Then Gabriel descended and informed him of what they were mocking and laughing at. He said to Ammar ibn Yasir, 'Go and ask them what they were laughing at, and say to them: May Allah burn you.' When he asked them and said, 'May Allah burn you,' they knew that a Qur'an had been revealed concerning them, so they began to make excuses to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. al-Jahir said, 'By Allah, I did not say anything; I only laughed in amazement at their words.' So He revealed His saying: ﴿Do not make excuses﴾ meaning Jadd ibn Qays and Wadi'ah, ﴿If We pardon a group of you﴾ meaning al-Jahir, ﴿We will punish a group﴾ meaning Jadd and Wadi'ah." This is the saying of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "A man among the hypocrites said, 'I have never seen anyone like these reciters of ours, who have the greatest appetite for food, who are the most lying, and the most cowardly at the time of battle,' meaning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions. Awf ibn Malik said to him, 'You lie, but you are a hypocrite; I will certainly inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.'" [p. 465] "He went to inform him, but found that the Qur'an had preceded him. So that man came and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, we were only engaging in idle talk and play.'" This is the saying of Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Aslam, and al-Qurazi.

The third: "A group of the hypocrites were traveling with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, 'If what this man says is true, then we are worse than donkeys.' So Allah informed His Prophet of what they had said, and ﴿And if you ask them﴾ was revealed." This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: "A man among the hypocrites said, 'Muhammad tells us that the camel of so-and-so is in such-and-such valley; what does he know of the unseen?' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: "Some hypocrites said, 'This man hopes to conquer the palaces and fortresses of Syria? Far-fetched!' So Allah informed His Prophet of that, and the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Hold the riders back for me,' and he came to them, and said, 'You said such-and-such.' They said, 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Qatadah.

The sixth: "Abdullah ibn Ubayy and a group with him used to say about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions what was not fitting. When it reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they said, 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play.' So Allah, Exalted is He, said: Say to them, ﴿Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾" This was said by al-Dahhak.

His saying: ﴿And if you ask them﴾ means: about what they were engaged in of mockery. ﴿They will surely say, "We were only engaging in idle talk and play"﴾ means: we were amusing ourselves with conversation. His saying: ﴿You have disbelieved﴾ means: your disbelief has become apparent after you had shown faith. This indicates that jest and play are equal in uttering a word of disbelief.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If We pardon a group of you﴾. The first: "Jadd ibn Qays, Wadi'ah ibn Khudham, and al-Jahir ibn Khamir were walking ahead of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on his return from Tabuk. Two of them began to mock the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while the third laughed at what the two were saying and did not speak anything. Then Gabriel descended and informed him of what they were mocking and laughing at. He said to Ammar ibn Yasir, 'Go and ask them what they were laughing at, and say to them: May Allah burn you.' When he asked them and said, 'May Allah burn you,' they knew that a Qur'an had been revealed concerning them, so they began to make excuses to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. al-Jahir said, 'By Allah, I did not say anything; I only laughed in amazement at their words.' So He revealed His saying: ﴿Do not make excuses﴾ meaning Jadd ibn Qays and Wadi'ah, ﴿If We pardon a group of you﴾ meaning al-Jahir, ﴿We will punish a group﴾ meaning Jadd and Wadi'ah." This is the saying of Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "A man among the hypocrites said, 'I have never seen anyone like these reciters of ours, who have the greatest appetite for food, who are the most lying, and the most cowardly at the time of battle,' meaning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions. Awf ibn Malik said to him, 'You lie, but you are a hypocrite; I will certainly inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.'" [p. 465] "He went to inform him, but found that the Qur'an had preceded him. So that man came and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, we were only engaging in idle talk and play.'" This is the saying of Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Aslam, and al-Qurazi.

The fourth: "A man among the hypocrites said, 'Muhammad tells us that the camel of so-and-so is in such-and-such valley; what does he know of the unseen?' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid.

So Allah informed His Prophet of that, and the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Hold the riders back for me,' and he came to them, and said, 'You said such-and-such.' They said, 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Qatadah.

When it reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they said, 'We were only engaging in idle talk and play.' So Allah, Exalted is He, said: Say to them, ﴿Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾" This was said by al-Dahhak.

His saying: ﴿And if you ask them﴾ means: about what they were engaged in of mockery. ﴿They will surely say, "We were only engaging in idle talk and play"﴾ means: we were amusing ourselves with conversation. **Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 9, verses 67–70:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are of one another.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: some of them follow the same religion as others. Muqatil said: some of them are allies of others, (they enjoin what is evil) meaning disbelief, ﴿and forbid what is right﴾ meaning faith.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: they withhold them from spending in the way of Allah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid. The second: they withhold them from every good, as said by Qatada. The third: they withhold them from striving (jihad) in the way of Allah. The fourth: they withhold them from raising them in supplication to Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Mawardi mentioned these two.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: they abandoned His command, so He abandoned them from His mercy and His guidance (tawfiq). He said: His saying ﴿they are sufficient for them﴾ means: it is the requital of their sins, just as you say: "I punished you according to your deed (hasb fi'lika)," and "the hasb of so-and-so is what befell him," meaning that is in proportion to his deed. The place of the kaf in His saying ﴿like those before you﴾ is in the accusative case, meaning: Allah promised you [punishment] for disbelieving in Him just as He promised those before you. Others said: He turned from speaking about them to addressing them directly, and compared them, in their deviation from His command, to those nations of the past who came before them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they enjoyed their share (khalaq)﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: they enjoyed their portion of the Hereafter in this world. Al-Zajjaj said: [they enjoyed] their share (hazz) of this world.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you plunged in﴾ meaning: into slandering the religion and denying your Prophet, just as they plunged in. ﴿Those, their deeds have become worthless in this world﴾ because they were not accepted from them, and in the Hereafter because they will not be rewarded for them. ﴿And those are the losers﴾ by forfeiting the reward and incurring the punishment.

(p-٤٦٨) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the people of Abraham﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: he means Nimrod ibn Canaan. (And the companions of Madyan) meaning the people of Shu'ayb. (And the overturned cities) are the towns of Lot. Al-Zajjaj said: they are the plural of mu'tafikah, the land overturned with them, meaning: it was turned upside down. He said: it is said that they are all those whom He destroyed, just as it is said of one who is ruined: "the world has turned against him."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ meaning these nations, ﴿but they denied them﴾. ﴿And Allah would not have wronged them﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He would not have destroyed them until He had sent among them a prophet to warn them. The meaning is that they were destroyed due to their deserving it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 71–72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another﴾. That is: some of them are allies (yuwali) of others, so they are as one hand, commanding what is good (bil-iman) and forbidding what is evil (al-kufr).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in gardens of perpetual residence (jannat ʿadn)﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: "In gardens of eternity (khuld). It is said: ʿadana fulan bi-ard kadha (so-and-so 'adana in such a land), meaning he settled there. From this comes al-maʿdin (the mine/place of origin), and His saying, ﴿in an assembly of truthfulness (maʿdin sidq)﴾, meaning in a firm foundation." He quoted al-Aʿsha:

"And if you seek hospitality from his forbearance, you will be hosted by a dignified man who has settled (ʿadana) [in nobility]."

That is: steady and not easily moved. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Jannat ʿadn is the middle (buṭnan) of Paradise, and its buṭnan is its center. It is the highest rank in Paradise, the abode of the Most Merciful, mighty and majestic. Its ceiling is His Throne. He created it with His own hand. In it is the spring of Tasnim, and the gardens surround it encompassing it."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and approval from Allah is greater﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Greater than what can be described." Al-Zajjaj said: "Greater than what they are in of bliss."

If it is said: Was approval not greater than bliss? There are two answers to this.

The first: the joy of the heart in the pleasure of the Lord is a bliss specific to the heart, and that is greater than the bliss of eating and drinking. In the hadith of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Allah, mighty and majestic, says to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise, are you content?' They say: 'Our Lord, and why would we not be content, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' He says: 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They say: 'And what is better than that?' He says: 'I shall bestow upon you My approval, and I shall never be displeased with you again.'"

The second: what necessitates the bliss is the approval, and what is necessitated is the fruit of what necessitates it, so the approval is the root.
