**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on Surah 9 (al-Tawbah), verse 97:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and most likely not to know the limits of what Allah has revealed﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Anna* (أنْ) is in the accusative position, because the *ba'* (الباء) has been omitted before *anna*. The meaning is: *ajdar* (أجْدَرُ) with regard to abandoning knowledge. You say: *jadir* (جَدِيرٌ) *an taf'ala* and *jadir bi-an taf'ala*, just as you say: *anta khalik* (خَلِيقٌ) *bi-an taf'ala*, meaning: this action is facilitated for you. If you omit the *ba'*, it is only correct with *an*. If you include the *ba'*, it is correct with *an* and with other than it, so we say: *anta jadir bi-an taqum* and *jadir bi-l-qiyam*. But if you say: *anta jadir al-qiyam*, it is an error. It is only correct with *an* because *an* indicates the future (الاستقبال), so it is as if it were a substitute (عِوَضٌ) for the omitted element." As for his saying (حُدُودَ ما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ), it means the lawful and the unlawful and the obligations. It has also been said: the intended meaning of the verse is that this applies to the majority of the Arabs.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 98:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who consider what they spend [in charity] as a loss﴾ — when they go out on a military campaign. It was also said: [it refers to] what he gives of the charity as a "maghram" (loss), because he does not hope for any reward for it. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-maghram (loss) is al-ghurm (penalty/loss) and al-khusr (ruin). Ibn Faris said: al-ghurm is that whose payment is obligatory, and al-gharam is the obligation, and the creditor (al-gharim) is so called because of his insistence. Others said: al-ghurm is the undertaking of what is not obligatory.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he waits﴾ — i.e., he awaits for you (bikum al-dawa'ir), i.e., the turns of time (dawa'ir al-zaman) with what is disliked: by death, or killing, or defeat. It was also said: [he awaits] the death of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the victory of the polytheists.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Upon them is the evil turn of fortune﴾ — Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a dammah on the sin (al-su').

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "al-sau'" with a fathah on the sin; and they recited likewise in Surat al-Fath (48:6). The meaning: upon them returns what they await for you of affliction. Al-Farra' said: the fathah on the sin in "al-sau'" is the usual form of speech. Whoever reads with a fathah intends the verbal noun from "sa'tuhu sau'an wa masa'ah" (I harmed him). Whoever reads with a dammah makes it a noun, as in your saying: "upon them is the turn of affliction and punishment." The sin may not be read with a dammah in His saying: ﴿What was your father not a man of evil (sau')﴾ [Maryam 19:28], nor in His saying: ﴿And you thought an evil (su') thought﴾ [al-Fath 48:12], because it is the opposite of your saying "a man of truthfulness (sidq)." And there is no meaning of "al-su'" here as punishment or affliction, so it is not read with a dammah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 99:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah﴾. Ibn Abbas said: They are those among the Bedouins who embraced Islam, such as Juhayna, Aslam, and Ghifar.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and take what they spend as means of nearness to Allah﴾ there are two opinions.

One is that it refers to jihad. The second is that it refers to charity. As for qurubat (means of nearness), it is the plural of qurba (nearness), which is that which brings the servant closer to Allah's good pleasure and love. Al-Zajjaj said: Regarding qurubat there are three readings: with a damma on the ra', with a fatha on it, and with it sukun-ed (qurubāt, qurabāt, and qurbāt). Regarding what is meant by ﴿the prayers of the Messenger﴾ there are two opinions.

One is his seeking forgiveness (istighfar), as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second is his supplication (du'a'), as said by Qatada, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj recited:

"Upon you is the like of what you have prayed, so close your eyes to sleep, for a man's side has a resting place."

He said: If you wish, you may say "mithla alladhi" and "mithlu alladhi". The matter is then an instruction to her to supplicate, as if he had said: Pray for me the like of what I prayed. The second meaning is: upon you is the like of this supplication.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely it is a means of nearness for them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "qurbatun lahum" with a light (sukun) pronunciation. Warsh, Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from Nafi', and Aban and al-Mufaddal, from Asim, transmitted "qurubatun lahum" with a damma on the ra'. Regarding what the pronoun refers to there are two opinions.

One is that the pronoun returns to their spending and their faith. The second is that it returns to the prayers of the Messenger.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will admit them to His mercy﴾. Ibn Abbas said: into His Garden.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ — concerning them there are six opinions.

The first: they are those who prayed towards both qiblas (the Jerusalem and the Ka'bah qiblas) along with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Sirin, and Qatadah.

The second: they are those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Pledge of Ridwan, which was at al-Hudaybiyah. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The third: they are the people of Badr. This was said by Ata' ibn Abi Rabah.

The fourth: they are all the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for precedence was attained by them through their companionship with him.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: Indeed Allah has forgiven all the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and made Paradise obligatory for them, both the good-doers among them and the wrong-doers, in His saying: ﴿And the foremost, the first⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿…

The fifth: they are the foremost by death and martyrdom, having preceded to the reward of Allah, exalted is He. Al-Mawardi mentioned this.

The sixth: they are those who embraced Islam before the Hijrah. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la mentioned this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ — Ya'qub read "wal-Ansari" with a raised ra' (i.e., "wal-Ansaru").

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and those who followed them in goodness﴾ — whoever says the foremost are all of the Companions makes these the Followers of the Companions, those who did not accompany the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It has been related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "and those who followed them in goodness" extends until the Hour arrives.

Whoever says they are the earlier ones among the Companions says: these followed them in their way and emulated them in their actions, so those were preferred by precedence, although companionship is attained by all. Ata' said: their following them in goodness means that they mention their virtues and invoke mercy upon them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿flowing beneath them are the rivers﴾ — Ibn Kathir read "min tahtiha" with an added "min" and a kasra on the second ta'.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is well pleased with them﴾ — this encompasses all of them. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah is pleased with their deeds, and they are pleased with what He has recompensed them with.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 9, Verse 101:**

(p-492)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: [They are] Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Aslam, Ghifar, and Ashja'. Among them, after their conversion to Islam, there were hypocrites. Muqatil said: Their dwellings were around Madinah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who have persisted in hypocrisy﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They became accustomed to it and remained steadfast in it. Among them were 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Jadd ibn Qays, al-Jullas, Mu'attib, Waw'ah, and Abu 'Amir al-Rahib. Abu 'Ubaydah said: They persisted in rebellion and became accustomed to it, and this is from their saying, "So-and-so became defiant (tamarrada)," and from it [comes the phrase] "a defiant devil" (shaytan marid).

If it is asked: How can He say, "And among the people of Madinah are those who have persisted," when in speech one may not say, "From the people, they sat"? There are three answers to this.

The first: the second "min" (مِن) is coordinated with the first, and the implied meaning is: "And among those around you of the Bedouins and among the people of Madinah are hypocrites." Then He began a new clause with "persisted" (مَرَدُوا).

The second: there is an implied "min" in the speech, its estimated form being: "And among the people of Madinah are those [min] who have persisted." So the "min" was omitted because the first "min" indicates it, as in His saying: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: "None except one who has a known station." According to this view, the speech ends at His saying "hypocrites."

The third: "persisted" (مَرَدُوا) is connected to "hypocrites," and the estimated meaning is: "And among the people of Madinah are hypocrites who have persisted." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these answers.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You do not know them﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

One: You do not know them, until We inform you of them. The second: You do not know their outcomes.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We will punish them twice﴾. Concerning this there are ten views.

The first: the first punishment is in this world, which is their exposure through hypocrisy, and the second punishment is the punishment of the grave. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up on a Friday, delivering a sermon, and said: 'O so-and-so, go out, for you are a hypocrite, and O so-and-so, go out,'" and thus he exposed them.

(p-493) The second: the first punishment is the enforcement of the prescribed penalties (hudud) upon them, and the second is the punishment of the grave. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: one of the two punishments is the zakat which is taken from them, and the other is the jihad to which they are commanded. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: hunger and the punishment of the grave. This was narrated by Shibl from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and Abu Malik also said this.

The fifth: hunger and killing. This was narrated by Sufyan from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

The sixth: killing and captivity. This was narrated by Mu'ammar from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. Ibn Qutaybah said: killing and imprisonment.

The seventh: they were punished with hunger twice. This was narrated by Khusayf from Mujahid.

The eighth: their punishment in this world is through calamities in their wealth and children, and in the Hereafter through the Fire. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The ninth: the first is at the time of death, when the angels strike their faces and their backs, and the second is in the grave with Munkar and Nakir. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

The tenth: the first is by the sword, and the second is at the time of death. This was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then they will be returned to a great punishment﴾, meaning the punishment of Hell.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 102:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, the scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed, in two opinions.

One of them: "They were ten men who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk. When the return of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew near, seven of them tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw them, he said, "Who are these?" They said, "This is Abu Lubaba and companions of his who stayed behind from you. They swore by Allah that they would not release themselves until you release them and excuse them." He said, "I also swear by Allah that I will not release them nor excuse them until Allah, may He be exalted, is the One who releases them. They turned away from me and stayed behind from the expedition with the Muslims." Then this verse was revealed, so he sent to them, released them and excused them." This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas. Al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas that those who stayed behind were six: Abu Lubaba tied himself up along with two men with him, and three remained who did not tie themselves up. When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) released them and excused them. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that they were three: Abu Lubaba ibn Abd al-Mundhir, Aws ibn Tha'laba, and Wadi'a ibn Khidham al-Ansari. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam said they were eight. Qatada said: it was mentioned to us that they were seven.

The second: it was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba alone. They differed concerning his sin, in two opinions.

One of them: that he betrayed Allah and His Messenger by his gesture toward the Banu Qurayza, when they consulted him about coming down under the judgment of Sa'd, that it was slaughter. This is the view of Mujahid, and we explained it under (al-Anfal: 27).

The second: that it was his staying behind from Tabuk. This was said by al-Zuhri. As for "al-i'tiraf" (acknowledgment), it is the affirmation of a thing from knowledge. Acknowledging one's sin is more conducive to the sincerity of repentance and its acceptance.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They mixed a righteous deed with another evil﴾. Ibn Jarir said: he placed the waw (and) in place of the ba' (with), and the meaning is: "with another evil," just as you say, "I mixed the water and the milk."

Concerning that deed there are two opinions.

One of them: the righteous deed is what preceded of their struggle (jihad), and the evil is their lagging behind from the jihad. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: the righteous deed is their repentance, and the evil is their staying behind. This was mentioned by al-Farra'. Concerning His saying "perhaps" (ʿasā), there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is obligatory from Allah, may He be exalted. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is a wavering for them between hope and apprehension, and that restrains from heedlessness and negligence.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 103:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, accepted the repentance of Abu Lubaba and his companions, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this is our wealth, so give charity from it on our behalf.' He said:

"I have not been commanded to take any of your wealth" (p-496), and then this verse was revealed."

Regarding "this charity" there are two opinions.

The first: it is the charity that they gave voluntarily. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and by the majority (al-jumhur). The second: it is zakat (obligatory alms), said by Ikrimah.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿purify them﴾. Al-Hasan recited "tutahhiruhum biha" with a jazm (sukun) on the ra'. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the words "tutahhiruhum" are a description (na't) of the charity, as if He had said: "Take from their wealth a charity that purifies." The more preferable view is that it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: "Indeed you purify them by it," and "fa-tutahhirhum" with the jazm, as a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr), meaning: "If you take from their wealth, you will purify them." With "tuzakkihim" it is not permissible except to write the ya', following the Mushaf (mushaf: the written codex). Ibn Abbas said: "tutahhiruhum" means from sins, and "watuzakkihim" means: you set them right (tuslihuhum). Regarding the words ﴿and pray for them﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: seek forgiveness for them, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: invoke (ud') for them, said by al-Suddi.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: "Inna salawatika" (Indeed your prayers). Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Nafi, Ibn Amir, and Abu Bakr from Asim recited "inna salawatika" in the plural. Hamza, al-Kisai, and Hafs from Asim recited "inna salataka" in the singular. Regarding the words ﴿is a comfort for them﴾ there are five opinions.

The first: a reassurance for them that Allah has accepted from them; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Abu Ubayda said: steadfastness and tranquility. The second: mercy for them, narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas. The third: nearness (qurba) for them, narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas. The fourth: dignity (waqar) for them, said by Qatada. The fifth: purification for them, related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: these are apart from the three who were left behind (alladhina khullifu).

(p-497) His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaʿlamū" with the yā', while ʿAbd al-Warith narrated "taʿlamū" with the tā'. As for His words: ﴿accepts repentance from His servants﴾, Abu ʿUbayda said: meaning "from His servants" (min ʿabīdihi); one says "akhadhtuhu minka" and "akhadhtuhu ʿanka" (I took it from you).

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and takes the charities﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: meaning He accepts them. Similar to it is ﴿Take what is easy of forgiveness﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 199], meaning: accept it.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And say: Work﴾. Ibn Zayd said: this is an address to those who repented.

(p-497) His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaʿlamū" with the yā', while ʿAbd al-Warith narrated "taʿlamū" with the tā'. As for His words: ﴿accepts repentance from His servants﴾, Abu ʿUbayda said: meaning "from His servants" (min ʿabīdihi); one says "akhadhtuhu minka" and "akhadhtuhu ʿanka" (I took it from you).

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and takes the charities﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: meaning He accepts them. Similar to it is ﴿Take what is easy of forgiveness﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 199], meaning: accept it.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And say: Work﴾. Ibn Zayd said: this is an address to those who repented.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 106:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And others are deferred﴾. Nafi', Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "marjawna" (مَرْجُونَ) without a hamzah.

The verse was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayyah, who were among those who stayed behind from Tabuk without an excuse. Then they did not go to great lengths in making excuses as Abu Lubabah and his companions did, and they did not bind themselves to the pillars. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) deferred their matter and forbade the people from speaking to them and mixing with them, until the saying of Allah was revealed: ﴿And [He turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118].

Al-Zajjaj said: "And others" is a conjunction with His saying, "And among the people of Madinah," so the meaning is: among them are hypocrites, and among them are (others who are deferred) – that is, held back. "Wa-immā" (وَإمّا, "either/or") indicates the occurrence of one of two things. Allah, Exalted is He, knows what their affair will end up as, but He addressed the servants in terms they understand, so the meaning is: let their matter be, for you, between fear and hope.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾, that is, All-Knowing of what their state will come to, All-Wise in what He does with them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who took a mosque﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-alladhina" with a waw, and it is likewise written with the waw in their codices. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "alladhina" without a waw, and it is likewise written without it in the codices of the people of Madinah and Syria. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with the waw, it is coordinated with what precedes it, like His saying: ﴿And among them is he who covenanted with Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:75], ﴿And among them are those who slander you﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:58], ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:61], and the meaning is: "And among them are those who took a mosque." As for whoever omits the waw, it is on two bases.

The first: that he supposes an omitted element, "And among them are those who took," like His saying: "Did you disbelieve?", meaning: it is said to them, "Did you disbelieve?"

The second: that he supposes the predicate to come afterward, as it is supposed in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Hajj 22:25], the meaning being: "He will take vengeance upon them and they will be punished."

The people of tafsir said: When the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf built the mosque of Quba', and sent to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he came to them and prayed in it, their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf, who were among the hypocrites of the Ansar, envied them and said: "We will build a mosque, and send to the Messenger of Allah so that he prays in it, and Abu 'Amir the monk prays in it when he comes from Syria." Abu 'Amir had become a monk in the Jahiliyyah and had adopted Christianity. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah, he opposed him, so he left for Syria and sent to the hypocrites: "Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, and build me a mosque, for I am going to Caesar to bring the army of the Romans and expel Muhammad and his companions." They built this mosque beside the mosque of Quba'. Those who built it were twelve men: Khudhdham ibn Khalid, from whose house the mosque was taken out; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Bijad ibn 'Uthman; Tha'labah ibn Hatib; Mu'attib ibn Qushayr; 'Abbad ibn Hunayf; Wadi'ah ibn Thabit; Abu Habibah ibn al-Az'ar; Jariyah ibn 'Amir, and his two sons Yazid and Mujammi'; Mujammi' was their imam in it, then his condition improved; and Bahzaj, grandfather of 'Abd Allah ibn Hunayf, who is the one to whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What did you intend by what I see?" He said: "By Allah, I intended only the good," and he was lying. Muqatil said: the one who swore was Mujammi'. It was said: they were seventeen. When they finished from it, they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "We have built a mosque for the one with an excuse, the one in need, and the rainy night, and we love that you come to us and pray in it." He called for his garment to put it on, and the Qur'an was revealed to him and Allah informed him of their news. So he summoned Ma'n ibn 'Adi and Malik ibn al-Dukhshum along with others, and said: "Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that it be made a dunghill where carrion is thrown. Abu 'Amir died in Syria, alone and a stranger.

As for the tafsir: al-Zajjaj said: "alladhina" is in the nominative position, meaning: "And among them are those who took a mosque for harm." "Diraran" is in the accusative as an object of purpose: the meaning is they took it for harm, disbelief, division and lying in wait. When the preposition was removed, the verb reached it and it took the accusative. The mufassirun said:

"Dirar" means causing harm to the mosque of Quba', "wa-kufran" means disbelief in Allah and His Messenger, "wa-tafriqan bayn al-mu'minin" means because they used to pray together in the mosque of Quba', so they wanted to split their congregation. "Al-irsad" means waiting; they waited there for the coming of Abu 'Amir, who had earlier waged war against Allah and His Messenger before the building of the mosque of harm. ﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended only the good"﴾, meaning: "We intended by building it only the good"; and in it are three aspects. The first: obedience to Allah. The second: Paradise. The third: doing what is better, namely establishing the religion and gathering for prayer. We have mentioned the name of the one who swore.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 108:

Allah's words: ﴿Do not stand in it﴾, meaning: do not pray in it ever. ﴿A mosque founded upon piety﴾, meaning: built upon obedience, and built by the God-fearing (from the first day), meaning: since the first day. Al-Zajjaj said: "Min" here is temporal, and the original particles are "mundhu" and "mudhu," which are the most common in usage. It is permissible for "min" to be used, because it is the basic particle for the beginning of a point in time and for partitive meaning. A similar usage is the verse of Zuhayr:

؎ To whom do the abodes belong at the summit of al-Hajar? Worn away by years and by months.

It was also said that its meaning is: since the passing of years and since the passing of a month. Regarding "this mosque," there are three views.

The first: it is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina, in which are his pulpit and his grave. Sahl ibn Sa'd narrated that two men disagreed during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the mosque that was founded upon piety [p-501]. One of them said: it is the mosque of the Messenger. The other said: it is the mosque of Quba'. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "It is this mosque of mine." This view was held by Ibn 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The second: it is the mosque of Quba'. 'Ali ibn Abi Talha narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, 'Urwa, Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil also held this view.

The third: it is every mosque built in Medina. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Allah's words: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾. The cause of its revelation was that some men of the people of Quba' used to cleanse themselves with water (istinja'), and this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them and said: 'What is it for which Allah has praised you?' They said: 'We cleanse ourselves with water.'" Based on this, the intended meaning is purification with water. Abu al-'Aliya said: "To purify themselves" means from sins.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 109:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who founded his building﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "asassa" with a fatha on the alif in both places and a fatha on the nun in both. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "ussisa" with a damma on the alif, and "bunyanuhu" with a raf' (damma) on the nun. Al-bunyan is a masdar (verbal noun) used to mean the thing built (al-mabni). Al-ta'sis (founding) is making the foundation (ass) of the building firm, and it is its origin. The meaning is: is the one who founds his building while being mindful of God, fearing Allah and hoping for His good pleasure better, or the one who founds his building while not being mindful? Al-Zajjaj said: wa-shafa al-shay' means he made its edge and its brink. Al-shafa, with a maqsur (short-vowel-ending form), is written with an alif, and its dual is shafawan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿on the brink of a crumbling bank﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "jurufin" with a heavy (fully vowelled) ra. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "jurfin" with a sukun on the ra. Abu 'Ali said: the damma is the original form, and the sukun is a lightening, like al-shaghl and al-shughl. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is "on the edge of a crumbling bank that falls." Al-jurf is what is undermined by floods from the valleys. Al-hair is that which falls; from it comes "tahawwara al-bannai wa-nhara," meaning the builder collapsed and crumbled when it fell. Ibn Kathir and Hamzah read "har" with a fatha on the ha. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr imala the ha. From 'Asim there are readings like both of these.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that it collapses with him﴾ into ﴿the fire of Hell﴾, that is, with the builder. Al-Zajjaj said: this is a parable, and the meaning is that the building of this mosque is like a building on the brink of Hell's pit, which will cause its people to collapse into it. Qatadah said: it was mentioned to us that they dug a pit in it, and smoke was seen rising from it. Jabir said: I saw the mosque that was built as harm (darar), and smoke was coming out of it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 110:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their building will not cease to be a cause of doubt in their hearts﴾, meaning the Mosque of Harm (masjid al-dirar) which they built. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: it is doubt and hypocrisy, because they used to think they were doing good in building it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is regret and remorse, because they came to regret its building. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

The third: the meaning is that the demolition of their building will remain a burning rancor and anger in their hearts. This was said by al-Suddi and al-Mubarrad.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾. Most readers recited "illa", which is the particle of exception. Ya'qub recited "ila an", making it a preposition (harf jarr). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited "tuqatta'a" with a dammah on the ta'. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Hafs from 'Asim recited "taqatta'a" with a fatah on the ta'. Then, regarding the meaning, there are two opinions.

One of them: "Unless they die." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and others.

The second: "Unless they repent with a repentance by which their hearts are cut to pieces through regret and grief over their negligence." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 111:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their souls﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that "when the Ansar (the Helpers) pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of 'Aqabah, and they were seventy men, 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish.' He said: 'I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and not associate anything with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect your own selves from.' They said: 'And if we do that, what will we have?' He said: 'Paradise.' They said: 'The sale is profitable; we will neither cancel it nor ask to cancel it.' So the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased. . .﴾, the verse." This was related by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. As for the purchase of the souls, it is through jihad.

Regarding the purchase of the wealth, there are two views. One of them: through spending in jihad. The second: through charities. The mention of "purchase" here is figurative (majaz, metaphorical usage), because the actual buyer is the one who does not own what is bought. It is like His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:245]. The meaning of the speech is that Allah commanded them to strive with their selves and their wealth, so that He would reward them for that with Paradise. He expressed this with the word "purchase" because it contains an exchange (ʿiwad) and a compensation (muʿawwad). Al-Hasan used to say: "No, by Allah, there is no believer in this world except that his pledge has been taken." Qatadah said: "He bargained with them, by Allah, and made the price high for them."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they kill and are killed﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read *fa-yaqtulūna wa-yuqtalūna* (they kill and are killed), with the active verb first and the passive second. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *fa-yuqtalūna wa-yaqtulūna* (they are killed and they kill), with the passive first and the active second. Abu 'Ali said: "The first reading means that they kill first and then are killed. The other reading may have the same meaning as the first, because a clause joined by the conjunction *wa* (and) may be intended to express sequence. If one does not assume sequence in it, then the meaning is: he kills those among them who remain after the killing of those who were killed, just as His saying: ﴿So they did not weaken for what befell them﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:146] means that those who remained did not weaken through the killing of those who were killed." The meaning of the speech is that Paradise is the compensation for their jihad, whether they killed or were killed.

*Wa'dan 'alayhi* (a promise binding upon Him): al-Zajjaj said: "*Wa'dan* (a promise) is in the accusative by way of meaning, because the meaning of His saying ﴿that for them is Paradise﴾ is ﴿a promise binding upon Him in truth﴾." He said: "His saying ﴿in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ indicates that the people of every religion were commanded to fight and were promised Paradise for it."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?﴾, meaning: there is no one more faithful to what He has promised than Allah. ﴿So rejoice﴾, meaning: be glad in this sale.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 112:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The repentant ones﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "When the preceding verse was revealed, a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, even if he steals, even if he commits adultery, even if he drinks wine?' So this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn Abbas. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: The nominative case (raf') is permissible here in several ways. The first is praise, as if he said: "These are the repentant ones," or "They are the repentant ones." It is also permissible that it be in apposition (badal), and the meaning would be: "The repentant ones fight." This is the view of the scholars of the Arabic language. But what I hold is that it is in the nominative by virtue of being a subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar, the predicate of a nominal sentence) is implied. The meaning is: "The repentant ones, and those mentioned with them, also have Paradise, even if they do not engage in jihad (struggle in the way of Allah), provided they do not intend to abandon jihad or to be obstinate, because some Muslims suffice for others in jihad."

The commentators differ regarding His saying "the repentant ones" in two views. The first: those who turn back from polytheism (shirk), hypocrisy (nifaq) and sins. The second: those who turn back to Allah in doing what He commanded and avoiding what He forbade.

Regarding His saying ﴿the worshippers﴾ there are three views. The first: those who obey Allah through worship, said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The second: those who establish the prayer, said by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas. The third: those who affirm the oneness of Allah (muwahhidun), said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the praisers﴾. Qatada said: They praise Allah in every state.

Regarding "the wanderers" (al-sa'ihun) there are four views. The first: those who fast, said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and others. Al-Farra' said: Those who consider the matter reflectively hold that the fasting person was called a wanderer only by way of comparison with the wanderer, because the wanderer has no provision with him. The Arabs say of a horse that stands with no fodder before it: "sa'im" (fasting). That is because it has two meals, morning and evening, so the fasting of the human being was likened to it, through his pre-dawn meal (suhur) and his breaking of the fast (iftar).

The second: that they are the warriors, said by Ata'. The third: that they are seekers of knowledge, said by Ikrima. The fourth: that they are the emigrants (muhajirun), said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿those who bow and prostrate﴾, meaning in prayer. ﴿Those who enjoin what is right﴾, which is obedience to Allah. ﴿And those who forbid what is wrong﴾, which is disobedience to Allah.

If it is said: What is the reason for the waw (and) entering into His saying "and those who forbid"? There are two answers regarding this.

The first: the waw entered here because it is the eighth attribute, and the Arabs join with waw to the seven, as in His saying: ﴿and their eighth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and His saying regarding the attributes of Paradise: ﴿and its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. This was mentioned by a group of the commentators.

The second: the waw entered on the forbidders because the one who enjoins what is right is also a forbidder of what is wrong in the state of his enjoining. So the entry of the waw indicates that enjoining what is right does not stand alone apart from forbidding what is wrong, just as the praisers stand alone in praise apart from the wanderers, and the wanderers in wandering apart from the praisers, in some states and times.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and those who guard the limits of Allah﴾. Al-Hasan said: those who uphold the command of Allah.

(p-507) **Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾.** There are four reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "When Abu Talib was on his deathbed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon him, and Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya were with him. He said, 'O uncle, say with me: There is no god but Allah, and I will plead for you with it before Allah.' Abu Jahl and Ibn Abi Umayya said, 'O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?!' They kept speaking to him until the last thing he said to them was, 'I am upon the religion of Abd al-Muttalib.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'I will certainly ask forgiveness for you for as long as I am not forbidden from you.' Then this was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe...﴾ up to the end of the verse, and this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whoever you love﴾ [al-Qasas 28:56]." Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it in the *Sahihayn* (the two Sahihs) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from his father.

It was also said: "When Abu Talib died, the Prophet (ﷺ) began to ask forgiveness for him. The Muslims said, 'What prevents us from asking forgiveness for our fathers and our close relatives, when Abraham asked forgiveness for his father? And this Muhammad asks forgiveness for his uncle?' So they asked forgiveness for the polytheists, and this verse was revealed."

Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Munadi said: "This is not sound. The Prophet (ﷺ) only said to his uncle, 'I will certainly ask forgiveness for you for as long as I am not forbidden from you,' before he died, (p-508) and this was in the context. As for his asking forgiveness for him after death, that is not so. This was reversed by the narrators, and the reversal remained."

The second: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by the grave of his mother Aminah, performed ablution, prayed two rak'ahs, then wept. The people wept at his weeping. Then he turned toward them, and they said, 'What made you weep?' He said, 'I passed by the grave of my mother, so I prayed two rak'ahs, then I asked my Lord permission to ask forgiveness for her, and I was forbidden. So I wept. Then I returned and prayed two rak'ahs, and I asked my Lord permission to ask forgiveness for her, and I was rebuked with a rebuke, and that made me weep.' Then he called for his riding-camel and mounted it. He had not gone far before the she-camel stood still due to the weight of the revelation, and then this was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe﴾ and the verse after it." Buraydah narrated it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The third: "A man asked forgiveness for his two parents, who were both polytheists. Ali ibn Abi Talib said to him, 'Do you ask forgiveness for them while they are polytheists?' He said, 'Did not Abraham ask forgiveness for his father?' Ali mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and then this verse and the one after it were revealed." Abu al-Khalil narrated it from Ali, peace be upon him.

The fourth: "Some men from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'O Prophet of Allah, among our fathers there were those who were good neighbours, who maintained family ties, who freed captives, and who fulfilled covenants. Should we not ask forgiveness for them?' He said, 'Yes, by Allah, I will certainly ask forgiveness for my father as Abraham asked forgiveness for his father.' Then this verse was revealed, and it explained the excuse of Abraham." This was said by Qatadah.

As for the meaning of His words: ﴿after it has become clear to them that they are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, that is: after it has become evident that they died as disbelievers.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

The first: Abraham had promised his father that he would ask forgiveness for him, and that is His words: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾ [Maryam 19:47]. He did not know that asking forgiveness for polytheists was forbidden until Allah informed him of that.

The second: His father had promised him that if he asked forgiveness for him, he would believe. Then when it became clear to Abraham that his father was an enemy of Allah the Exalted, by his dying in disbelief, he abandoned praying for him. According to the first view, the pronoun in "iyyahu" (him) refers to Azar, and according to the second view, it refers to Abraham. Ibn al-Sumayfa', Mu'adh al-Qari', and Abu Nahik read: "wa'adaha abahu" with the letter *ba'* (i.e., the promise was made by the father).

Concerning *awwah* (the one who laments much): there are eight views.

The first: that he is one who is humble in supplication and beseeches earnestly. Narrated by Abdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: that he is one who supplicates much. Narrated by Zirr from Abdullah, and Ubayd ibn Umayr said the same.

The third: that he is the compassionate. Narrated by Abu al-Ubayd ibn al-Amiri from Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Abu Maysarah said the same.

The fourth: that he is the one certain (of Allah). Narrated by Abu Dhabyan from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid, Ata', Ikrimah, and al-Dahhak said the same.

The fifth: that he is the believer. Narrated by al-Awfi, Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

(p-510) The sixth: that he is the one who glorifies (Allah). Narrated by Abu Ishaq from Abu Maysarah, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Jubayr said the same.

The seventh: that he is the one who sighs in lamentation at the mention of Allah's punishment. This was said by al-Sha'bi. Abu Ubayda said: "The figurative sense of *awwah* is the figurative sense of *fa''al* from *ta'awwuh* (sighing), and its meaning is: one who is humbly submissive out of compassion and fear, and who is constant in obedience to his Lord." Al-Muthaqqib said:

*"When I rise to saddle her at night, she sighs the sigh of a grieving man."*

The eighth: that he is the jurist (faqih). Narrated by Ibn Jurayj from Mujahid. As for *halim* (forbearing), it is the one who pardons sins.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verses 115–116:

The saying of Allah, ﴿And Allah would not misguide a people﴾ and the verse continues. Its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul): "When the verse of the inheritance shares (ayat al-fara'id) was revealed, and abrogation (naskh) came, and some people who had known the earlier command, such as the command concerning the qibla (direction of prayer) and wine (khamr), were absent, and some groups died upon that, they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and this verse was revealed." This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas.

Some people said: the meaning is that He made clear that He would not seize them for seeking forgiveness for the polytheists (mushrikin) before it was prohibited. So when He prohibited it and they did not refrain from it, then they went astray.

Ibn al-Anbari said: in the verse there is omission (hadhf) and abbreviation (ikhtisar), and the interpretation is: "until (p-511) it becomes clear to them what they should guard against, so they do not guard against it. At that point they deserve misguidance." So he omitted what he omitted for the clarification of its meaning, as the Arabs say: "I ordered you to trade, so you earned wealth" (أمَرْتُكَ بِالتِّجارَةِ فَكَسَبَتَ الأمْوالَ), meaning: "so you traded and earned."

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verses 115–116:

The saying of Allah, ﴿And Allah would not misguide a people﴾ and the verse continues. Its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul): "When the verse of the inheritance shares (ayat al-fara'id) was revealed, and abrogation (naskh) came, and some people who had known the earlier command, such as the command concerning the qibla (direction of prayer) and wine (khamr), were absent, and some groups died upon that, they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and this verse was revealed." Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 117:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾. The exegetes said: He turned to him in forgiveness regarding his permission to the hypocrites to stay behind. The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: this is a key phrase (miftah kalam), because when it was the cause of the repentance of those who repented, it was mentioned along with them, like His saying: ﴿And know that one-fifth of whatever you obtain as spoils belongs to Allah and to the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿who followed him in the hour of hardship﴾. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian and exegete) said: they are those who followed him in the expedition of Tabuk. What is meant by "the hour of hardship" is the time of hardship, because "hour" (sa'a) applies to all time. At that time there was intense heat, and the people were in severe distress. A camel was shared among a group who rode it in turns, and they were in poverty, so two people would sometimes divide a single date, and a group would sometimes suck on a date so that they could drink water after it, and they would sometimes slaughter camels and drink from the water in their stomachs because of the heat. "It was said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: Tell us about the hour of hardship. He said: We set out for Tabuk in intense summer heat, and we stopped at a place where we were struck by thirst, until we thought our necks would be cut off. A man would go seeking water and not return until he thought his neck would be severed, and a man would slaughter his camel, squeeze its dung and drink it, and put what remained on his liver. Abu Bakr said: O Messenger of Allah, Allah has accustomed you to good in supplication, so supplicate for us. He said: "Do you like that?" He said: Yes. So he raised his hands, and did not lower them until the sky gave rain, and they filled what they had with them. Then we went out to look, and we did not find that it had passed beyond the army."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾. Hamzah and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "yazigu" (kada yazigu) with the ya'. The rest read it with the ta'. There are three opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

The first: they were inclined to stay behind from him, and they were people from among the Muslims who intended that, then they caught up with him. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the hearts inclined to return because of the hardship they faced, but they did not swerve from faith. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: the hearts nearly perished (tal'af) through exertion and hardship. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness﴾. He repeated the mention of repentance, because the beginning of the verse does not mention their sin, so He mentioned repentance first as a favour from Him, then mentioned their sin, then repeated the mention of repentance.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 118:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [He also forgave] the three who were left behind﴾. Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, al-Sha'bi, and Ibn Ya'mur read "khalafu" with an alif (khālafū). Mu'adh al-Qari', 'Ikrimah, and Humayd read "khalafu" (khalafū) with a fatha on the kha and a light lam. Abu al-Jawza' and Abu al-'Aliyah read "khallafu" (khallafū) with a fatha on the kha and a shadda on the lam. These are the ones meant by His saying: ﴿And others [are] deferred﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:106], and their names have already been mentioned. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of "khullifu" (were left behind).

The first: they were left behind from repentance (tawbah). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. So the meaning is: they were left behind from Allah's acceptance of repentance toward Abu Lubabah and his companions, since they did not humble themselves as those did.

The second: they were left behind from the expedition of Tabuk. This was said by Qatadah. Their account is included within the repentance of Ka'b ibn Malik, and I have narrated it in the book "al-Hada'iq."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Until, when the earth grew constricted for them despite its vastness﴾. That is: it became constricted despite its spaciousness. This is because the Muslims shunned them, refrained from dealing with and speaking to them, and were commanded to separate from their wives, while the Prophet ﷺ turned away from them. ﴿And their souls constricted within them﴾ through worry and grief. (And they thought) that is: they became certain ﴿that there is no refuge﴾, that is: no protection from Allah and His punishment except Him. ﴿Then He turned to them [in forgiveness]﴾; He repeated the turning (tawbah) for emphasis. ﴿That they might repent﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that they might remain upright. Others said: He enabled them to repent so that they would persist in it and not return to what would nullify it. Someone was asked about sincere repentance (tawbah nasuhah) and said: it is that the earth becomes constricted upon the one who repents, and his own self becomes constricted upon him, as with the repentance of Ka'b and his two companions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions.

One of them: it was revealed concerning the story of the three who stayed behind. (p-514) The second: it concerns the People of the Book. The meaning would be: O you who have believed in Moses and Jesus, fear Allah regarding your belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), and be with the truthful.

Regarding what is meant by "the truthful," there are five opinions.

The first: that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions. This was said by Ibn 'Umar.

The second: Abu Bakr and 'Umar. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak. Ibn al-Sumayfa', Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Mu'adh al-Qari recited "maʿa al-ṣādiqayn" with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the nun, in the dual form.

The third: that they are the three who were left behind, who were truthful to the Prophet (ﷺ) about their delay. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: that they are the Muhajirun, because they did not stay behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in jihad. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: It has been said that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq argued with this verse on the day of Saqifa. He said: O assembly of the Ansar, Allah says in His Book: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Those are the truthful﴾ [al-Hashr: 8]. Who are they? The Ansar said: You are they. He said: Then Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾, so He commanded you to be with us, and He did not command us to be with you. Therefore we are the leaders and you are the ministers.

The fifth: that it is general in meaning. This was said by Qatadah. Here "maʿa" (with) carries the meaning of "min" (from/among). Likewise it is in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-kūnū min al-ṣādiqīn" (and be among the truthful).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verses 120–121:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It was not for the people of Madinah and those of the Bedouins around them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: It means Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ashjaʿ, Aslam, and Ghifar. ﴿Nor to prefer themselves over his own self﴾ — meaning, they should not be content to seek ease and comfort for themselves while the Messenger of Allah is in heat and hardship. It is said: "raghibtu bi-nafsi ʿan al-shay'" (I held myself above a thing) when I elevate myself above it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That﴾, i.e., that prohibition against remaining behind, ﴿is because they will not suffer thirst﴾, which is thirst, ﴿nor fatigue﴾, which is weariness, ﴿nor hunger﴾, which is famine, ﴿nor do they incur any loss against an enemy﴾, whether captivity, killing, or defeat. Allah informed them that He will reward them for all of that.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor do they spend any expenditure, small or large﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a date or more than that. ﴿Nor do they cross a valley﴾, going forward or returning, ﴿except that it is written for them﴾, i.e., their reward for that is recorded for them, ﴿that Allah may reward them with the best﴾, i.e., with the best ﴿of what they used to do﴾.

Section

Our shaykh ʿAli ibn ʿUbaydullah said: The exegetes differed regarding this verse. One group said: At the beginning of the matter, it was not permissible to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when jihad was obligatory upon everyone; then this was abrogated (nasakh) by His saying: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. (p-516) Another group said: Allah, exalted is He, made it obligatory upon all believers during the time of the Prophet ﷺ, those who had no excuse, to go out with him for two reasons:

The first: It is obligatory upon them to protect him with their own selves.

The second: When the Messenger went out, the whole religion went out with him, so they were commanded to support one another so that the number would not decrease. This ruling remains in effect until our time; so if the Commander of the Faithful goes out to jihad, it is obligatory upon the general body of Muslims to follow him, for the reason we have mentioned. Based on this, the verse is muhkam (non-abrogated). Abu Sulayman said: Every verse has its own meaning, and there is no way to claim abrogation (naskh) for either of the two verses.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 122:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are four reports.

The first: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed the faults of the hypocrites at the expedition of Tabuk, the believers said: 'By Allah, we will never again stay behind from any expedition that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) undertakes, nor from any detachment ever.' Then, when he sent out the detachments after Tabuk, the Muslims all went forth together and left the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alone, so this verse was revealed." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against Mudar, their lands became barren, so a tribe from among them would come to Madinah with all its people, out of hardship, while displaying Islam while lying, and they strained the circumstances of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so this verse was revealed." Ibn Abi Talhah related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "Some people embraced Islam and went out to the desert to teach their people, so there was revealed: (p-517) ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you﴾ [at-Tawbah: 39]. Some of the hypocrites said: 'Whoever from the desert dwellers does not go forth is doomed,' so this verse was revealed." This was said by Ikrimah.

The fourth: "Some people went out to the desert to teach the people and guide them, and to gather from the firewood what would benefit them. The people said to them: 'We see you have only left your companions and come to us.' So all of them returned from the desert, and this verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid.

Az-Zajjaj said: The wording of the verse is the wording of a statement, but its meaning is a command, like His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [at-Tawbah: 113]. The meaning is: it is fitting that some of them go forth and some remain.

Al-Farra' said: "yanfiru" and "yanfuru" (with the fa' vowelled with kasra or damma) are two dialectal forms.

The exegetes differed concerning the intended meaning of this "nafir" (going forth), on two views.

The first: it is going forth to the enemy. The meaning is: it is not for them to go forth all together; rather, a group goes forth, and a group remains with the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿That they may gain understanding in the religion﴾, meaning the group who remain behind. When the detachments return, and a revelation has descended after they left or a matter has newly arisen, they inform those who stayed and warn them of it when they return to them. This meaning is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is going forth to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): a group from among them goes forth so that those who go forth may gain understanding, and so that they may warn their people who stayed behind. This is the saying of al-Hasan, and it is closer to the apparent sense of the verse. According to the first view, the going forth of this group is with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) if he sets out on a raid or with his detachments. According to the second view, the going forth of the group to the Messenger of Allah is for acquiring knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah al-Tawbah (9), verses 123–126:

One view is that they are the Romans; this was said by Ibn 'Umar. The second is Qurayzah, al-Nadir, Khaybar, and Fadak; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The third is the Daylam; this was said by al-Hasan. The fourth is the Arabs; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The fifth is that it is general, concerning fighting the nearest of the nearby; this was said by Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj said: In this verse there is evidence that the people of every frontier (thaghr) should fight those who are adjacent to them. He said: It has also been said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would sometimes skip over the enemies adjacent to him in his warfare, so that this would be more awe-inspiring for him. So he commanded fighting those nearest to him, so that this would become a precedent (yustann bi-dhalika)."

As for ghilzah (غِلْظَةٌ, "harshness"), there are three vocalizations: ghilzah, with a kasrah on the ghayn, which is the reading of most reciters; ghalzah, with a fatha on the ghayn, transmitted by Jabalah from 'Asim; and ghulzah, with a dammah on the ghayn, transmitted by al-Mufaddal from 'Asim. Similar forms are: jadhwah, jidhwah, and judhwah (a burning coal); wajnah, wijnah, and wujnah (cheek); raghwah, righwah, and rughwah (foam); rabwah, ribwah, and rubwah (elevated ground); qaswah, qiswah, and quswah (hardness); and alwah, ilwah, and ulwah (oath). A ewe that is lajbah, lijbah, or lujbah is one whose milk has dried up. Ibn 'Abbas said, regarding His words "ghilzah": it means courage. Mujahid said: it means severity.

God Most High says: ﴿Among them is one who says, "Which of you has this increased in faith?"﴾ This is the statement of the hypocrites to one another, mocking the word of God Most High. ﴿As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith﴾ because, when they affirm it and act upon what is in it, it increases them in faith. ﴿And they rejoice﴾ meaning they are glad at its revelation. ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ meaning doubt and hypocrisy.

Regarding what is meant by rijs (filth, "uncleanness") there are three views.

The first is doubt; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is sin; this was said by Muqatil. The third is disbelief, because whenever they disbelieved in a surah its disbelief increased; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

God Most High says: ﴿Do they not see?﴾ meaning the hypocrites. Hamzah recited "Do you not see?" with the letter ta' (tarawna), addressing the believers. Regarding the meaning of yaftinun (they are tested), there are eight views.

The first is that they tell a lie or two by which they mislead; this was said by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

The second is that they become hypocrites, then believers, then hypocrites again; this was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third is that they are afflicted by fighting in the way of God; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The fourth is that they are tested by drought and hunger; this was said by Mujahid.

The fifth is by pains and illnesses; this was said by 'Atiyyah.

The sixth is that they break their covenant once or twice; this was said by Yaman.

The seventh is that they disbelieve, because whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them of what they had said when they were alone, they knew that he was a prophet; then Satan would come to them and say, "He only received this from you," and so they would associate partners with God. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

The eighth is that they are disgraced by the manifestation of their hypocrisy; this was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

God Most High says: ﴿Then they do not repent﴾ meaning from their hypocrisy. ﴿Nor do they remember﴾ meaning they take heed and are admonished.

(p-520) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them look at others﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Whenever a surah was sent down containing the faults of the hypocrites, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed them and alluded to them in his sermon, this was hard for them, and some of them would look at others, wanting to escape, saying: ﴿Does anyone among the believers see you if you get up?﴾ If no one saw them, they would leave the mosque."

Al-Zajjaj said: It is as if they said this by gesture, so that no one would notice them, "then they turned away" from the place, and it is possible that they turned away from acting upon what they heard.

Al-Hasan said: "Then they turned away" with a determination to deny Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he had brought.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has turned their hearts away﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: from faith. Al-Zajjaj said: He led them astray as a recompense for their action.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 128:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read the fa' with a damma. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Muhaysin, and Mahbub from Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha. Regarding the one with a damma (anfusikum, "from among yourselves"), there are four opinions.

The first: from all of the Arabs. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no tribe among the Arabs except that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has been born into it."

The second: from among those you know. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: from a marriage in which nothing of the births of the Jahiliyyah touched him. This was said by Ja'far al-Sadiq.

(p-521) The fourth: a human being like you, which is more emphatic as proof, because you understand from one who is like you. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Regarding the one with a fatha (anfasikum), there are three opinions.

The first: the best of you in character. The second: the most noble of you in lineage. The third: the most obedient of you to Allah, mighty and majestic.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It grieves him what distresses you﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: it is hard upon him what troubles you. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: "It is hard upon him, your distress (ʿanatakum), and al-'anat is meeting with hardship."

The second: it is hard upon him what leads you into sin. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He is eager over you﴾. Al-Hasan said: "He is eager over you that you believe."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To the believers he is kind and merciful﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He named him with two of his names." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Ra'uf" is fa'ul, from ar-ra'fah, which is softer than ar-rahmah; it is also said "ra'uf," and he recited:

*You see for the believers over you a right like the deed of the father who is kind (ra'uf) and merciful.*

It was also said: kind (ra'uf) to the obedient, merciful to the sinners.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 9, verse 129:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, they turn away from faith, ﴿then say: "Allah is sufficient for me; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne."﴾ That is, He suffices me. ﴿Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾.

Ibn Muhaysin recited "al-'Azimu" (the Mighty) with a nominative ḍamma on the mīm (i.e., "al-'Azīmu," as a grammatical adjective of the Lord in the nominative case). The Throne is singled out for mention because it is the greatest, and so the smaller things are included within it.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: The last verse revealed was ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ to the end of the surah. Complete, by the help of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, is the third part of "Zad al-Masir fi 'Ilm al-Tafsir" (Provision of the Journey in the Science of Exegesis), and it is followed by the fourth part, whose beginning is the tafsir of Surah [Yunus].
